bio.p: Mark Swanson received his PhD in physics from the University of Missouri at Columbia in 1976 under the supervision of Justin Huang. After postdoctoral appointments at the University of Alberta and the University of Connecticut he held a faculty appointment at the University of Connecticut at Stamford from 1983 to 2014, during which time he spent six years in university administrative roles. He is the author of 25 research articles and four monographs, with an emphasis on field theory and path integral techniques. He is currently Emeritus Professor of Physics at the University of Connecticut and lives in Monroe, Connecticut.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Classical Field Theory and the Stress-Energy Tensor (Second Edition) is an introduction to classical field theory and the mathematics required to formulate and analyze it. The development of the mathematical formalism, previously in an appendix, is integrated into the presentation of the physical concepts. The book develops the core concepts of field theory by applying Newtonian physics to the stretched string, emphasizing the relationship between fields and the observer's coordinate systems and using basic concepts of differential geometry and functional techniques. This collection of insights should be invaluable to both the student, instructor, and active researcher since it presents a unified view of field theories without the added complication of quantization.
• A logical and thorough development of both the mathematics and physics of classical fields.
• A unified theme based on the relationship of fields, coordinate transformations, and the stress-energy tensor.
• Applications to a wide set of areas and phenomena where classical field theory yields important physical insights.
• An accessible introduction for the student and a useful reference for the researcher.

• A significant number of worked examples will be added to each chapter of the new edition. These will be combined with a set of problems with suggestions to the reader how to approach solving them and whose answers will be provided.

sec.title: Preface
sec.p: While it is fair to say that the last century of physics has been dominated both experimentally and theoretically by the study of quantum processes, the framework for the understanding of these phenomena consists of concepts developed in classical physics and extended to quantum mechanical systems. In that regard, the necessity of generalizing the concepts of energy, momentum, and angular momentum to the case of classical fields provided many of the tools used in the wave-particle duality of quantum mechanics. Classical electrodynamics and nonabelian gauge theories have become successful quantum field theories, yielding deep insights into quantum processes. At the time of this writing, developing a quantum mechanically consistent version of gravitation is a vigorous and unsettled area of research, yet the insights provided by Einsteinʼs classical theory of general relativity remain the basis for much of the effort to create such a theory.

The purpose of this monograph is to present a reasonably concise introduction to the key concepts of classical field theory. Its intended audiences are beginning graduate students and advanced undergraduate students who wish to study the unifying structures and physical insights provided by classical field theory without dealing with the additional complication of quantization. In that regard, there are many important aspects of field theory that can be understood without quantizing the fields. These include the action formulation, Galilean and relativistic invariance, traveling and standing waves, spin angular momentum, gauge invariance, subsidiary conditions, fluctuations, spinor and vector fields, conservation laws and symmetries, and the Higgs mechanism, all of which are often treated briefly in a course on quantum field theory. In writing such a monograph, there are many decisions to be made about the level of presentation and the choice of topics and examples. I have chosen to assume the reader has a good working knowledge of undergraduate Newtonian mechanics and electricity and magnetism. This includes the Newtonian formulation of mechanics, the formulation of Maxwellʼs equations in terms of a vector and scalar potential, and a brush with special relativity and its relationship to these two areas. It assumes no background in continuum mechanics and fluid dynamics, spinor fields, general relativity, nonabelian gauge theories, differential geometry, or group theory. The intent is to connect these diverse areas together in terms of variational principles, conservation laws and symmetries, coordinate transformations, and the insights given by the stress–energy tensor. In so doing, pedagogical goals have superseded a rigorous mathematical presentation. This stems from my belief that presenting these connections succinctly with clear and reasonably basic examples will extend the readerʼs understanding much more quickly and effectively than pointing out the sometimes bewildering subtleties that require a more rigorous approach. However, one topic that is present throughout the monograph is the nature of wave disturbances in the classical fields, and it serves to both unite and differentiate the various field theories treated.

It is the intention of this monograph to assist the reader in gaining a basic foundation in the structures and concepts commonly used in classical field theory. The references and recommended reading listed at the end of each chapter have been chosen from books and research papers I have found useful for further study of the details and applications presented in the chapter. It is my sincere hope that the reader will use the recommended texts for further study of the myriad details and applications that classical fields possess, as well as eventually proceeding to the study of quantum field theory. Because this monograph is primarily pedagogical in nature and designed to cover a wide variety of topics, most of the original research papers in classical field theory are, with a few exceptions, not listed. I sincerely apologize to the giants of physics, both living and dead, whose research, insights, and hard work laid the foundations of field theory, but a proper list of their papers would be extremely long and largely irrelevant to the intended goal of the monograph. In that regard, some concepts presented in this text have become so widely used that they are known simply by the name of their originator, and this form of attribution is followed whenever possible.

The second edition of this monograph has given me the opportunity to more clearly develop and integrate the mathematical tools useful in analyzing classical field theory and to weed out the errors of the first edition. It is assumed the reader has a working knowledge of multivariable calculus and some experience solving simple differential equations, along with some acquaintance with matrix algebra. The book presents an overview of those mathematical ideas and techniques used in field theory that may be unfamiliar to the intended reader, when and where they are essential to the development of the physical concepts. The revised version begins with an introduction to the concepts of differential geometry, since it undergirds classical field theory and especially general relativity. It then develops variational techniques and their application to classical physics, along with a brief overview of Fourier series and transforms, the Dirac delta, and their relationship to solving differential equations. Field theories consistent with Newtonian mechanics and Galilean relativity are derived and used to develop basic concepts present in all field theories. These include the continuum mechanics of the stretched string and fluid motion. Complex variable techniques are introduced in the context of complex fields that can be used to describe classical aspects of the Bose–Einstein condensate, as well as serving as the basis of quantum wave mechanics. A review of linear algebra and an introduction to Lie group theory present the mathematical tools to develop classical relativistic field theory. An advanced reader may wish to skip the review sections covering these topics and use the monograph as a reference for these ideas, while the introductory reader can obtain an overview of these essential areas of mathematics, identifying those topics that may require further study. These concepts are used to develop the representations of the Lorentz group that provide the types of relativistic fields. These include scalar fields, spinor fields, the vector field of electrodynamics, and the metric tensor version of gravitation, including both the theory and selected applications. A final chapter presents the classical aspects of nonabelian gauge theories and the briefest of introductions to string theory. All of these are presented without mathematical rigor and aimed at the level of understanding appropriate to the intended audience.

sec.title: Mark S Swanson
sec.p: Photo courtesy of Nancy Ruth Levine.

Mark Swanson received his PhD in physics from the University of Missouri at Columbia in 1976 under the supervision of Justin Huang. After postdoctoral appointments at the University of Alberta and the University of Connecticut, he held a faculty appointment at the University of Connecticut at Stamford from 1983 to 2014, during which time he spent six years in university administrative roles. He is the author of 25 research articles and three other monographs with an emphasis on field theory and path integral techniques. He is currently Emeritus Professor of Physics at the University of Connecticut.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The term field has its origins in characterizing the action of forces between spatially separated material objects. It was first used by Faraday in the context of electricity and magnetism, although the earlier work of Euler describing fluid flow as well as the description of the propagation of waves through a medium used similar concepts. In order to be the agent of action at a distance between material objects, a field must exist throughout a volume of space and evolve over time. Because a field can be present throughout a volume of space, it is very different from the Newtonian concept of a material point particle, which always has a definite position at a given time. Newtonʼs laws of motion describe how a particle responds to forces and how it reacts back on the agents of those forces. Newtonʼs laws and their subsequent formulation in terms of a variational principle give rise to the generalized concepts of energy and momentum as well as conservation laws. However, Newtonʼs laws of motion do not predict or explain what forces exist in nature, how they are transmitted, or if they are fundamental or the secondary result of other more fundamental forces. Answering these questions requires the interaction of experiment and theory. In that process, it became apparent to 19th-century physicists that the field concept was central to the mathematical description of electric and magnetic phenomena. This culminated in the development of Maxwellʼs equations, a cornerstone of modern physics as well as a guidepost to understanding the nature of fundamental forces.

Because physical phenomena do not come with a coordinate system or clock, observers must choose a coordinate system to describe the location and a clock to record the time at which their observations occur. Once a coordinate system for spatial position
r
and time t is chosen, a field is represented by a mathematical function of
r
and t. At the foundation of physics is the axiom that the choice of coordinate system cannot affect the physical laws of nature, although the choice can clearly affect how observations of those physical laws are reported. At the inception of modern physics it was also recognized that relative motion plays a profound role in the observation of physical phenomena. The mathematical quantity that represents the field must therefore have a well-defined set of rules for how it changes or transforms when a different coordinate system is chosen or when relative motion between different observers is present. These rules allow observations quantified by different observers to be compared or related to each other. The set of rules for comparing observations in different coordinate systems or coordinate systems in relative motion therefore goes by the generic term relativity. These requirements need considerable further explanation, but eventually lead to the identification of the possible types of mathematical quantities that can be used to represent fields, as well as the imposition of restrictions on the types of field theories that can be formulated.

In the process of developing field theory it will be seen that a field contains energy, momentum, and angular momentum that is distributed throughout a volume of space. In addition, a field may serve as an agent that transmits force by interacting with material objects, and in so doing may transfer energy, momentum, and angular momentum to the object. It is therefore necessary to generalize the Newtonian concepts of energy and momentum to include the contributions from both fields and particulate matter. It will be seen that each field is associated with a contribution to what is commonly called the stress–energy tensor, and it is the stress–energy tensor which quantifies the energy and momentum present in the field. It is often the case that a field theory predicts the existence and nature of waves associated with the field. Waves are the manifestation of energy and momentum moving through a volume of space in the form of the field. In the case of electricity and magnetism, the wave was identified as light, giving rise to physical optics. It was the experimental study of light propagation that revealed a flaw in Newtonian physics. In order to remedy this flaw, it was necessary to allow the relative motion between two observers to affect the way in which those two observers measure distances and time intervals, leading to the special theory of relativity. The subsequent generalization to observers in arbitrary relative motion led to the general theory of relativity, in which gravitation is the result of the interaction of space and time with mass and energy, with the latter quantified by the stress–energy tensor.

It is often said that classical physics would govern a world where Planckʼs constant
ℏ
is zero. Strictly speaking, this is true, since the quantum mechanical deviations from Newtonian physics and its relativistic version can be characterized in terms of powers of
ℏ
. Maxwellʼs equations and Einsteinʼs general theory of relativity have no explicit reference to
ℏ
and can therefore be analyzed with no reference to
ℏ
. However, ignoring field theories with an explicit dependence on
ℏ
in their constants overlooks the contribution that the techniques of classical field theory can provide for such theories. Classical field techniques give an important perspective on the energy and momentum content of such theories, as well as the nature and meaning of the conservation laws these theories obey. As a result, the techniques and results of classical field theory can often shed light on a field theory that requires
ℏ
in its definition. An example of this will be found in chapter 5, where a classical version of Bose–Einstein condensation is examined by treating the nonlinear Schrödinger equation as a classical field theory.

The first step in formulating a field theory is to choose the mathematical quantities that will represent the field. These are chosen from the set of possible mathematical functions whose transformation properties allow different observers to relate their observations. The second step is to determine how these quantities can reflect the physical phenomena and interactions being observed. Because fields are functions of space and time, the process of cataloging the possible types of fields first requires an understanding of the geometric properties of coordinate systems and their relation to the space the coordinate system is describing. Subsequently, the relationship between different coordinate systems will determine the mathematical quantities that can represent the fields present in the space. It is also critical to understand how physical laws affect the relationship between different observers, in particular observers in relative motion, and how this also determines the types of fields that are consistent with physical laws. In addition, classical field theory must have a clear relation to Newtonian physics and its modifications for consistency with special relativity and general relativity. In that regard, the mathematical foundation for field theory is multivariable calculus and its extensions into differential geometry, partial differential equations, and group theory. In an effort to be complete, this text will attempt to provide the reader with a physics perspective on these relevant mathematical topics. In the process it is hoped that the reader will gain an appreciation of the remarkable intellectual achievement that classical field theory represents, as well as understanding how it forms the foundation of quantum physics.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Properly formulating classical field theory requires some basic concepts from differential geometry. This book will develop these ideas and techniques specifically for application to physical systems, and so the presentation is neither complete nor rigorous. Instead, the intent is to place physical concepts familiar from basic physics into a more unified context. In particular, coordinate systems, coordinate transformations, vectors, the metric tensor, the gradient, the Laplacian, and differential forms are critical ingredients in formulating classical field theory and also form the foundation of basic differential geometry. These ideas and constructs will be used throughout this book and so familiarity with these tools is important.

sec.title: Manifolds
sec.p:
Newtonian physics was formulated to describe the phenomenon of motion or dynamics. The classical dynamics of Newton makes a number of assumptions, often taken for granted in the presentation of elementary physics, regarding the properties of the space in which motion occurs. The most basic assumption of Newtonian physics is that the space available for motion is a smooth collection of points and that, as a point particle moves in that space, its position is a continuous or smooth trajectory through those points. It is therefore possible to install a coordinate system, at least locally, that allows the definition of the calculus operations of differentiation and integration. Loosely speaking, the term local means that there is a neighborhood of each point where this is possible. The installation of a coordinate system is understood to be a local mapping of the points in the space into the coordinates of the point or a function that meets the same objective. There may be overlapping neighborhoods with different coordinate systems, and where they overlap these coordinate mappings must be invertible and one-to-one, which requires their differentiability. A collection of points is referred to mathematically as a manifold, generically designated

, and so such a smooth collection of points is known as a differentiable manifold. This brief description leaves out many subtleties, and the reader interested in a more mathematically rigorous development of manifolds is referred to one of the many excellent books on modern analysis.

Classical physics typically assumes that the spatial manifold where motion occurs possesses three independent dimensions or directions. Although motion may be restricted to a two-dimensional plane or a one-dimensional line, in general, the motion of a Newtonian particle is a three-dimensional phenomenon. Modern physics has relaxed this assumption to allow the consideration of physical manifolds that are n-dimensional. Stated simply, this means there are n independent directions available for motion. This step was required to accommodate the concept of four-dimensional space-time, but has also emerged in the context of higher-dimensional attempts to unify forces, such as Kaluza–Klein theory and string theory. The physics of Newton and contemporaries further assumed that both space and time, equivalently distance and duration, were absolute properties of the world that all observers could agree upon. A significant offshoot of that worldview was the assumption that three-dimensional Euclidean geometry correctly describes the relationships between points in the spatial manifold of motion. A manifold where Euclid’s axioms and theorems hold will be referred to as Euclidean. It was understood that Euclidean geometry did not hold on a curved surface, such as the surface of the Earth, and so Euclidean manifolds are often referred to as flat manifolds. The n-dimensional extension of the Euclidean plane is known mathematically as
R
n
, where n copies of the real line
R
serve as the Euclidean degrees of freedom.

However, experimental observations and the subsequent development of the special and general theories of relativity forced a revision of both these assumptions. In particular, the special theory of relativity showed that the measurements of distance and time intervals by different observers are affected by their relative motion, and that correctly describing motion required merging space and time into the four-dimensional manifold referred to as space-time. Further, the principle of general relativity incorporates a description of gravitation in terms of a space-time that is dynamic and non-Euclidean, so that distances as well as durations are no longer governed by Euclidean geometry. These changes required a significant revision of Newtonian physics as well as a fundamental overhaul of how physical theories are formulated.

An effective presentation of classical field theory must therefore take into account the changes in assumptions regarding the manifold for motion and fields that have occurred over the last century. Although space, together with time, are still assumed to define a differentiable manifold, understanding both the arbitrary dimensionality and the deviation from Euclidean behavior benefit greatly from adopting the more flexible techniques of modern differential geometry. Some of these techniques may be unfamiliar, and so this chapter will present a simplified introduction to the more unified approach to manifolds, coordinates, and vector spaces that basic differential geometry provides. The standard Euclidean treatment of manifolds and vectors is still contained in this approach, but it allows the generalizations required by modern classical field theory.

sec.title: Coordinate systems
sec.p: Quantifying position and motion in a differentiable manifold requires a choice of coordinate system. This consists of choosing an origin point and mapping the points of the manifold onto a coordinate grid around the origin. Figure 1.1 depicts the same point in two commonly used coordinate systems for the two-dimensional Euclidean plane. The choice of coordinate system and origin is arbitrary, and it is stressed that coordinate systems themselves have no physical meaning. However, once a coordinate system is chosen, the coordinates of a point in the space around the origin are determined by its place on the coordinate grid in relation to the origin.

caption.p: Cartesian and polar coordinate grids.

sec.p:
In two dimensions Cartesian coordinates consist of two straight perpendicular lines or coordinate axes through the origin and a coordinate grid consisting of straight lines parallel to these two axes. The Cartesian coordinates
( x , y )
of a point are defined by parallel projection, and the two gridlines that determine the position of a point form a parallelogram with the coordinate axes. The point of intersection of the line with the axis gives the coordinate of the point. For the choice of two-dimensional polar coordinates the grids consist of circles of radius r around the origin coupled with radial lines at each angle θ. The polar coordinates of the point are then given by
( r , θ )
. In order for the two coordinate systems to share the same neighborhood of the manifold, they must be related by differentiable and invertible functions. If the plane is Euclidean, these relations are given by the familiar Euclidean expressions, 1.1

sec.title: The Jacobian
sec.p: A coordinate system may result in ambiguous or undefined coordinates for some points. An example occurs at the origin in polar coordinates, where the polar angle is arbitrary and therefore undefined. For the sake of brevity this book will only peripherally touch on such subtleties and instead assume that the coordinate system provides unambiguous and unique coordinates for all but a few points. In that regard, the coordinate transformation is invertible at all points where the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation is nonzero.

So far, there have been no restrictions on the specific form of the coordinate transformation other than giving a nonzero value for the Jacobian (1.12). In physical applications, there is a significant possibility that a coordinate transformation may involve two coordinate systems whose origins are in relative motion. Understanding the effects of relative motion for different observers requires a physical principle for resolution. This is because relative motion involves the interplay of time and distance measurements, and may result in effects similar to those of forces. This will be discussed in detail later.

sec.title: Vectors and direction vectors
sec.p:
The spatial relationship of two points in a manifold allows the definition of a vector, a quantity with both direction and magnitude. While vectors can be defined between any two points in the manifold, initial attention will be given to the position vector of a point p. In the case of a Euclidean manifold, it is defined as an oriented straight line or arrow from the origin to the point p, with the latter point referred to as the vector tip. The position vector therefore has both a direction as well as a magnitude given by its length. It is denoted in boldface as
r
p
, but the p is often dropped and
r
is then understood to be the position vector of an arbitrary point in the manifold. In the x-coordinate system the position vector will be a function of the coordinates of the point p, and so it will often be written
r
(
x
p
)
or
r
( x )
for an arbitrary point.

It is important to note that the position vector lies in the manifold, and if the manifold is non-Euclidean, the position vector is not a straight line in the traditional Euclidean sense. As an example, the position vector on a sphere can be visualized as an arrow emanating from the north pole and coinciding with a segment of a longitude line that intersects the point of interest. The longitude gridlines are great circles on the sphere and correspond to the spherical version of a straight line. In a general non-Euclidean manifold the space between the origin and the point of interest is not flat and, unlike the sphere, may not even be uniformly curved. Determining the length between the origin and the point is therefore more difficult and renders the finite position vector a far less useful concept for a non-Euclidean manifold. However, in the Euclidean case, the straight-line position vector is uniquely determined by the choice of origin and the point defining the vector tip. It is important to note that using different coordinate systems does not alter the Euclidean vector
r
p
as long as the two coordinate systems share the same origin.

It is worth repeating that a finite position vector
r
can be expressed in the general form (1.35) or the specific Cartesian form (1.33) only in a Euclidean manifold. This is possible because a Euclidean manifold allows unique straight lines everywhere throughout the manifold. As a result, specifying the origin and the point of interest in a Euclidean manifold is sufficient to determine the unique straight line between the two, in turn defining the finite position vector. However, in a general non-Euclidean manifold, only the infinitesimal change in the position vector
d
r
p
, which is defined at each point p by (1.32), is available. This is because the orientation of the unit vectors at each point will depend on the curvature of the manifold at that point. As a result, the components of the vector will depend upon the nature of the manifold between the origin and the final position as well as the path between the two points. In a non-Euclidean manifold, finite position vectors become cumbersome and so are seldom, if ever, used. Alternate methods for determining distances and angles will be developed.

Because of the similarity between (1.55) and the law of cosines, vector addition is often depicted as placing one vector on the tip of the other vector and drawing the third leg of the triangle that is formed. This is consistent with the intuitive idea that adding the two position vectors is identical to performing sequential displacements and determining the final position from vector addition. However, both vectors in (1.55) and (1.56) are defined with respect to the same origin. As a result, forming a triangle, or equivalently a parallelogram, requires the second position vector to be moved or transported to the tip of the other position vector so that it remains parallel to itself, a process known as parallel transport. Parallel transport in a Euclidean manifold is straightforward, while the parallel transport of vectors in a non-Euclidean manifold will be developed in chapter 10.

Like the Kronecker delta, the Levi-Civita symbol is a mathematical construct and therefore coordinate independent. Result (1.101) is therefore an identity that can be used in defining coordinate invariant expressions involving the Levi-Civita symbol. The left-hand side of identity (1.101) shows that the Levi-Civita symbol can be treated as a covariant tensor of rank n under a transformation, but requires an additional factor of the inverse of the Jacobian of the transformation. This is an important aspect of defining coordinate invariant expressions involving the Levi-Civita symbol, since the factor of the Jacobian that appears can be used to cancel Jacobian factors generated by other quantities. A quantity whose transformation involves the Jacobian of the transformation is referred to as a tensor density, and the power of the Jacobian determines its weight. sec.title: Trajectories and tangent spaces
sec.p:
So far, attention has primarily been focused on position vectors, either the infinitesimal version
d r
of (1.32) or the finite version
r
of (1.35). Regardless of whether the manifold is Euclidean or not, the metric tensor relation (1.64) associates a distance in the manifold with position vectors, i.e. either infinitesimal position changes or, by integration, finite distance vectors. However, vectors may be present at every point in the manifold that are independent of the choice of an origin. Examples from Newtonian physics include the force acting on a particle or its velocity when it is located at a specific point. Since force and velocity have both a magnitude and direction, they must be represented by a vector at that point.

( t )

In what follows the parameter t will be referred to as the time, for the moment ignoring any issues around its units. Since there is a nondenumerable infinity of trajectories that pass through point p, the set of all possible tangent vectors at point p given by (1.107) forms a space of vectors that are tangent to the manifold

at the point p. The term vector space means that any two vectors belonging to the space can be combined through addition and scalar multiplication, so that a linear combination of any two tangent vectors at a point results in a vector that is also tangent to the point. As a result, the space of vectors defined in this manner is referred to as the tangent space at the point p and is denoted by

(  )

However, the definition of (1.107) shows that the vectors in the tangent space of a point can be expressed in terms of the same basis direction vectors used to describe the position vector, either finite or infinitesimal, at the point. The tangent space therefore has the same dimension as the manifold, which means that any vector in the tangent space at a point can be expanded as a linear combination of the normalized direction vectors at the point. This is because the direction vectors are also tangent to the manifold


sec.title: The vector product
sec.p:
A second form of vector multiplication, known as the cross or vector product, defines a vector that is orthogonal to a collection of other vectors. The version of the vector product presented in this section will be specific to three spatial dimensions. A related definition of the vector product for higher dimensions is given in a later section. The vector product is quite often used in three-dimensional quantities, such as angular momentum and the Lorentz force. However, it is less useful in arbitrary dimensions and has largely been superseded by the wedge product to be discussed later in this chapter. sec.title: The gradient
sec.p:
The relationship between direction vectors and partial derivatives is encapsulated in the gradient, a key mathematical tool in both differential geometry and field theory. The gradient, denoted

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In order for the mathematical rules that govern fields and material particles to constitute a complete theory, the physical quantities defined in Newtonian physics, such as momentum and energy, must be generalized to include the contributions from fields. For that reason it is useful to review Newtonian physics in the context of basic differential geometry, and this starts with Newtonian particle trajectories and their relationship to vectors and vector fields. Functional methods are then introduced to formulate the variational approach to Newtonian mechanics. It is the variational approach that can be generalized to field theory.

body.p: In order for the mathematical rules that govern fields and material particles to constitute a complete theory, the physical quantities defined in Newtonian physics, such as momentum and energy, must be generalized to include the contributions from fields. For that reason it is useful to review Newtonian physics in the context of basic differential geometry, and this starts with Newtonian particle trajectories and their relationship to vectors and vector fields. Functional methods are then introduced to formulate the variational approach to Newtonian mechanics. It is the variational approach that can be generalized to field theory.

sec.title: Newton’s first law and Galilean relativity
sec.p: In Newtonian physics the time t is treated as a parameter that characterizes the motion along a trajectory. It is treated as an absolute quantity provided experimentally by a mechanical device generically referred to as a clock. All Newtonian observers of physical phenomena are equipped with identically functioning clocks which remain synchronized throughout their observations of phenomena. Similarly, Newtonian physics measures distances with a second device generically referred to as a meter stick that remains identical throughout all motion, and all observers are equipped with identical meter sticks. Therefore, in Newtonian physics, all observers agree upon the time intervals between events as well as the distances separating material objects at any given moment. For the purpose of comparing or relating observations made by two different observers, the origins of two different coordinate systems can be thought of as the positions of two distinct observers watching the motion of some point mass m. The respective coordinate systems serve as reference frames, or simply frames, for the two observers who record the positions of events with respect to the origin as well as the time of occurrence. An example of an event is the presence of an object at a particular location at a particular time. The rules for relating observations made by the two different observers are referred to as relativity and these rules play a critical role in determining physical laws.

Newton’s first law, the law of inertia, states that an object will remain in uniform unaccelerated motion if zero total force acts upon it. While the Galilean transformations yield a family of inertial frames where there will also be zero total force, in 1632 Galileo argued that consistency with experiments required that the universal laws of motion take the same form in all inertial frames. In that regard, Newton’s second law of motion is formulated to be consistent with what is now called the Galilean principle. In modern terms the ability to change coordinate systems in specific ways and not affect the form of the equations of motion is referred to as a symmetry. Result (2.36) is the Galilean rule for velocity addition, which demonstrates that two inertial observers can refer their velocities to a third reference frame as long as that third frame is also an inertial frame. The Earth is commonly used as such a reference frame in elementary physics, but it is not a true inertial frame, since the Earth is both orbiting the Sun and rotating about an axis relative to the fixed stars. Both of these rotational motions involve a centripetal acceleration, and therefore a reference frame embedded in the Earth is not a true Galilean inertial frame. In Newtonian mechanics the acceleration associated with a reference frame that is rotating relative to a true inertial frame creates apparent forces, or pseudoforces, such as the Coriolis force, similarly to the appearance of the pseudoforce

These are distinguished from pseudoforces that do not possess an agent, which is another material body, that creates them. Such pseudoforces are discussed in classical mechanics texts.

sec.title: The action approach to Newtonian mechanics
sec.p:
Modern Newtonian mechanics and classical field theory are formulated in terms of a variational or action principle. This approach has the advantage of revealing the relationship between conservation laws, such as energy and angular momentum, and the symmetries of the system’s action, such as translational or rotational invariance. This relationship will be defined and explored in detail throughout this book. The equations of motion, which generalize Newton’s second law (2.1), are then generated by applying the techniques of the calculus of variations to extremize the action. abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In this chapter the fundamental concepts and tools for formulating and analyzing field theory are developed by applying Newtonian mechanics to a uniform horizontally stretched string. In particular, analyzing the stretched string yields the generalization of the Newtonian concepts of energy and momentum to continuous systems, encapsulated in the stress–energy tensor. It also quantifies the emergence of waves, representing the motion of momentum and energy through the medium of the string. In this simple case, the field quantifies the disturbance of the stretched string away from its equilibrium or zero kinetic energy configuration. The advantage of this simple example is that it merges basic Newtonian mechanics and the concept of the field.

body.p: In this chapter the fundamental concepts and tools for formulating and analyzing field theory are developed by applying Newtonian mechanics to a uniform horizontally stretched string. In particular, analyzing the stretched string yields the generalization of the Newtonian concepts of energy and momentum to continuous systems, encapsulated in the stress–energy tensor. It also quantifies the emergence of waves, representing the motion of momentum and energy through the medium of the string. In this simple case, the field quantifies the disturbance of the stretched string away from its equilibrium or zero kinetic energy configuration. The advantage of this simple example is that it merges basic Newtonian mechanics and the concept of the field.

sec.title: The mechanical properties of a stretched string
sec.p: The mechanical properties of a uniform stretched string are critical to formulating its behavior when it is disturbed from its equilibrium configuration. Consideration begins with a uniform string of mass M consisting of two segments, each with a length L. The string is horizontally stretched between two end points by an arbitrary but uniform tension F . Since the tension creates a force that has an opposite direction at each end of the string, it is understood that F is the magnitude of the force at each end. The agent creating this tension is external, such as weights attached over a pulley at each end of the string or the tuning key of a guitar. It is assumed that the string can stretch slightly but that the tension remains constant during this process. This is an approximation since the tension in the string will change as it is stretched or a load is placed on it. This is discussed again in the last two sections of this chapter, where the weight of the string itself results in a varying tension in the string and affects the static shape of the string. As depicted in figure 3.1, the potential energy of the string is revealed by suspending a mass m from its midpoint and allowing it to descend to a distance h below the horizontal equilibrium shape of the string.

sec.p:

sec.title: Solving the Euler–Lagrange equation
sec.p:
Obtaining a unique solution to (3.22) requires an appropriate set of boundary conditions. In general, the necessary boundary conditions follow from the fact that the equation of motion (3.22) is a second-order hyperbolic partial differential equation. In order to understand what constitutes sufficient boundary conditions to specify a unique solution, the string can be viewed as a sequence of point masses or segments, each of which is governed by Newton’s equation of motion. Because Newton’s second law is a second-order differential equation, the jth segment requires two boundary conditions. In the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions the height
φ
j
of the jth segment is specified at t = 0 and t = T. In the continuum limit for the stretched string, Dirichlet boundary conditions therefore correspond to the spatial shape of the string at those two times. As discussed earlier Dirichlet boundary conditions correspond to specifying

A propagating disturbance in a medium is the original definition of a wave and accurately describes many material waves, such as water waves and sound waves. In the case of the string the motion of the medium is perpendicular or transverse to the direction of the wave as it passes a point, and so it is referred to as a transverse wave. In some cases, such as sound, the motion of the medium is parallel to the direction of the wave as it passes a point and such waves are referred to as longitudinal. In both cases the wave disturbance is governed by (3.22), and so (3.22) is commonly referred to as the wave equation. While (3.22) was obtained for the case of a stretched string, the wave equation and its modified forms occur in many physical systems governed by field theories. It is therefore important to investigate its basic properties.

sec.p: Prior to the experimental study of electromagnetic waves, all known wave phenomena exhibited the property that an observer in motion relative to the wave medium observed velocities of propagation that obeyed Galilean relativity. This reinforced both the concept of waves as a disturbance that propagates through a medium and the belief that Galilean relativity governed the observed velocities of propagation. It will be seen in chapter 6 that Maxwell’s equations give rise to an electromagnetic wave governed by the d’Alembertian equation with a velocity of propagation that matches the speed of light. However, it was experimentally found that observers in relative motion measured the same velocity of light in all directions, in direct contradiction to Galilean relativity. This was ultimately resolved by simultaneously replacing Galilean relativity with special relativity and abandoning the concept of a medium for light waves.

sec.title: Momentum and energy in field theories

sec.title: The stress–energy tensor
sec.p:
Results (3.71), (3.72), and (3.76) were obtained for the specific case of the stretched string. Results (3.78) and (3.79) used specific properties of solutions to the equation of motion in the rest frame of the string. sec.title: Static sources and Green’s function techniques
sec.p:
In this section the result of attaching a static source of disturbance to the stretched string is analyzed from a field theory point of view. In its simplest version, a static pointlike mass m is fixed to the string at the horizontal position x = a, where
0 < a < L
. The weight mg of the point mass causes the string to sag, resulting in a displacement φ of the string away from equilibrium. The point particle therefore acts as a source of the field φ, which measures the vertical displacement of the string away from horizontal. This mechanism is similar to those that occur in other field theories, where point masses and charges act as a source of the field in the space around them, allowing the field to transmit force and energy to other masses or charges.

This problem can be solved using elementary physics techniques and the result can then be compared to that obtained using field theory techniques. It is assumed the string sags by a distance h under the weight mg, while its ends remain fixed and its two segments remain straight. As mentioned in the first section of this chapter, the two straight segments depicted in figure 3.3 will require different tensions to be at equilibrium. sec.title: The catenary, the Beltrami identity, and constraints
sec.p:
As was the case in the previous section, field theories are often analyzed for static solutions. These solutions provide useful information about the behavior of the medium and the nature of disturbances away from equilibrium that do not propagate. These solutions typically occur in field theories where there are interaction terms in the Lagrangian density. In the case of a stretched string considered in the previous sections, the string was assumed to maintain both a uniform mass density μ and a uniform tension F. Clearly, this is valid only if the disturbance away from equilibrium is small, which was the assumption made in deriving the potential (3.7). In the previous section the gravitational interaction term
V
( φ )
= μ g φ
( x )
was added to the potential energy density. Its presence led to the stationary shape of a parabola for the string, described by equation (3.113). However, this result was contingent on the assumptions of uniform tension and uniform mass density, which in turn require only small deviations from equilibrium.

The case of large deviations from equilibrium can be considered for the case of a suspended string. The tension will not be uniform as the string sags under the effect of its weight. Instead, the tension will vary with position and will be determined by the equations of motion. This is depicted in figure 3.4.

sec.p: The Poisson bracket for classical theory carries over into quantum field theory, where it becomes the commutator of the fields and their canonical momenta. With slight modifications, the Poisson bracket formalism can be adapted to all the field theories that will be treated in this book.

•
Lanczos C 1970 The Variational Principles of Mechanics 4th edn (New York: Dover)
•
Goldstein H, Poole C and Safko J 2000 Classical Mechanics 3rd edn (San Francisco, CA: Addison-Wesley)
•
Thornton S and Marion J 2004 Classical Dynamics of Particles and Systems (Boston, MA: Cengage)
•
Soper D 2008 Classical Field Theory (New York: Dover)
Monographs dealing exclusively with continuum mechanics include
•
Truesdell C and Noll W 2003 The Non-Linear Field Theories of Mechanics 3rd edn (Berlin: Springer)
Monographs that focus on solving the wave equation include
•
Freegarde T 2013 Introduction to the Physics of Waves (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Mathematical monographs presenting methods for solving partial differential equations include
•

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: A fluid is, by definition, a substance that flows, which means that it responds to pressure differences and forces with the motion of its constituent mass. Despite being a familiar phenomenon on the everyday level, fluid dynamics has remained a mathematically difficult and incomplete subject since the seminal work of Euler in the 18th century. Using Euler’s approach, fluid dynamics consistent with Newtonian physics can be developed by treating the velocity v of the fluid at position r at time t as the velocity field v( r , t). This allows a straightforward derivation of the Euler equation and the Navier–Stokes equation, with their numerous applications to fluid flow. However, such an approach ignores the atomic or microscopic properties of the matter making up the fluid, instead using the macroscopic or bulk properties of the fluid, such as density, viscosity, and bulk modulus

body.p:
A fluid is, by definition, a substance that flows, which means that it responds to pressure differences and forces with the motion of its constituent mass. Despite being a familiar phenomenon on the everyday level, fluid dynamics has remained a mathematically difficult and incomplete subject since the seminal work of Euler in the 18th century. Using Euler’s approach, fluid dynamics consistent with Newtonian physics can be developed by treating the velocity
v
of the fluid at position
r
at time t as the velocity field
v
( r , t )
. This allows a straightforward derivation of the Euler equation and the Navier–Stokes equation, with their numerous applications to fluid flow. However, such an approach ignores the atomic or microscopic properties of the matter making up the fluid, instead using the macroscopic or bulk properties of the fluid, such as density, viscosity, and bulk modulus. The alternative is to use a statistical approach in which a distribution function
f (
v
, r , t )
gives the number of identical pointlike atoms or molecules with the velocity
v
at point
r
at time t. Such a microscopic statistical approach leads to the Boltzmann–Vlasov equation and allows the bulk properties of fluids, such as pressure and viscosity, to be defined in terms of the distribution function augmented by the mean free path between atomic collisions. Such an approach also allows the eventual derivation of the Navier–Stokes equation by using the mean or average velocity of the atoms as the Eulerian velocity field
v
( r , t )
. In this monograph the Newtonian approach to fluid dynamics will be followed, since, like the stretched string considered in chapter 3, it allows an action approach to deriving the equations of motion for fluid flow. In turn, this allows the stress–energy tensor for perfect fluids to be defined from the action, in keeping with the central themes of this monograph. The diligent reader should consult the bibliography to find one of the excellent monographs where the statistical approach is presented.

sec.title: Fluid flow from Newtonian physics
sec.p:
At the macroscopic level, the two generic forms for a fluid are liquid and gas. A liquid is characterized by maintaining its volume while flowing, while a gas is characterized by expanding to fill the volume available to it. These two phases are governed by the equation of state for the substance. In the macroscopic approach to fluid flow, liquids are often characterized by being incompressible, so that their density remains constant, while gases are compressible and have variable densities. The macroscopic approach to fluid flow therefore requires using the scalar density field,
ρ ( r , t )
, which gives the mass per unit volume at position
r
at time t. It describes the flow in terms of a velocity or vector field,
v
( r , t )

r

Relation (4.18) is known as the Euler equation in recognition of Euler’s groundbreaking work on fluid flow in the 18th century. It provides three first-order partial differential equations, but contains at least four unknowns, the density ρ and the three components of the velocity field
v
. It is also nonlinear since it possesses a quadratic term in the velocity. As a result, unlike the stretched string result (3.30), solutions to (4.18) do not obey the principle of superposition, and this increases the difficulty in solving (4.18).

The presence of pressure in (4.18) often requires knowledge of the equation of state for the fluid, and it is important to note that the pressure
P ( r , t )
has been defined locally in each element of the fluid, since it is the spatial variation of the pressure that contributes to (4.18). To complicate matters further, the equation of state for the fluid can result in the pressure being dependent on the absolute temperature T, which can also vary with position. For example, the perfect gas law is given by
P ( r , t ) = ρ ( r , t ) R
T ( r , t )
, where R is the perfect gas constant. It is also necessary to assume that the equation of state holds locally within an element of the fluid. As a result, the temperature may not be uniform throughout the body of the fluid, which means that the fluid is not in thermal equilibrium and heat conduction is occurring. It follows that solving (4.18) may therefore require the inclusion of thermodynamic processes where mechanical energy and heat are exchanged locally as a result of temperature gradients, resulting in non-equilibrium processes within the fluid and between the fluid and its environment. Modeling these processes require further properties of the fluid, such as its specific heat and thermal conductivity, as well as specifying its environment. This is discussed in somewhat more detail in the coming sections dealing with viscosity and thermodynamics. The upshot is that modeling fluid flow often results in a complicated and in many cases insolvable set of equations. In order to make progress in extracting analytical information from (4.18), it is often necessary to make simplifying assumptions, such as the presence of uniform pressure and temperature, the incompressiblity of the fluid, the absence of angular momentum in the flow, or that the flow is reversible. These simplifying assumptions will be discussed in the section on applications.

sec.title: The equation of continuity
sec.p:
Solving the Euler or Navier–Stokes equations typically requires additional mathematical relationships. One such additional relationship is obtained by considering the rate at which mass is changing in a volume. Mass is conserved in almost all terrestrial fluids, but it is not conserved in the event that nuclear processes are taking place. As a result, mass conservation does not hold in the core of a main sequence star where nuclear fusion converts mass into thermal energy and radiation. sec.title: Viscosity
sec.p: A dissipative force of great importance in the flow of fluids is quantified by the viscosity of the fluid. When adjacent layers of a fluid move at different speeds, referred to as shearing, a dissipative force akin to friction appears between the layers that opposes their motion. This property of the fluid is referred to as shearing viscosity. At the microscopic level this viscous force is created by the transport of momentum via atomic diffusion between adjacent layers of the flowing fluid and can be modeled in the statistical approach to fluids in terms of atomic collisions converting mechanical energy into the random energy of heat. In the macroscopic description of fluids it is necessary to introduce a shearing viscosity coefficient η, which is measured by separating two perfectly smooth plates of area A by a vertical distance h and placing a thin layer of the fluid between them.

If a constant F is applied tangentially to the top plate, it will reach a terminal velocity
v
that is proportional to F as it slides on the layer of fluid separating it from the stationary bottom plate. Similarly, if the top plate has the velocity
v
parallel to the bottom plate, there is a force F of resistance to the motion acting tangentially on the top plate that is found to be proportional to
v
. It is the latter situation that is depicted in figure 4.3. For a Newtonian fluid the coefficient of shearing viscosity η is defined as 4.35
η =
Fh
v
A

and is roughly constant for fixed temperatures. There are many materials, such as plastics and suspensions, for which (4.35) does not hold, and these are referred to as non-Newtonian fluids. These will not be considered here. The units of η are the same as momentum per unit area, which is consistent with viscosity being the result of diffusion of momentum between sliding layers of fluid. Of course, the tangential drag force F due to viscosity is opposite to the direction of the upper plate’s motion. For the case that the top plate has the mass m and slides with an initial velocity
v
o , Newton’s second law shows that, in the absence of other forces, viscosity causes exponentially damped motion, 4.36

This situation also occurs in elementary mechanics problems when kinetic friction is present and acting in opposition to an object’s motion. Result (4.36) does not indicate how to account for the loss of kinetic energy, only that nonzero viscosity results in it. Like kinetic friction in mechanics, the presence of viscosity prevents an action approach to analyzing fluid flow, since this would require the inclusion of the exchange of heat with the fluid’s environment as well as the flow of heat within the fluid due to temperature gradients. However, the effects of viscosity can be included in the Navier–Stokes equation (4.19) as a contribution to the unspecified force density
f

sec.title: Basic solutions to the Navier–Stokes equation
sec.p: Although a general analytic solution to the Navier–Stokes equation (4.54) for an imperfect fluid is currently unavailable, it is possible to make simplifying assumptions that allow it to be solved for special situations. It is often the case that the fluid can be treated as incompressible, particularly liquids with a large bulk modulus. It is also possible to limit consideration to a steady or time-independent flow. This section will consider only simple cases and will avoid unresolved issues such as turbulent flow.

sec.p:
The specific value of R and the boundary conditions for the system determine the behavior of the velocity field and the vorticity. Scaling the two equations has revealed that the characteristic length and velocity will combine with the viscosity and density of the fluid in a dimensionless way in the solution of the two original equations (4.54) and (4.97). Therefore, if two systems share the same Reynolds number and the same boundary conditions, then their velocity field and vorticity will behave identically. This allows the experimental analysis of a small system and extrapolation of the result to a similar large system with the same Reynolds number. This is the principle used in wind tunnels, where scaled-down models of aircraft and wings are tested for their behavior in flight. For such a case, L is given by the flow distance across the actual wing and V is the aircraft’s expected average airspeed. If L

The nature of the flow described by the scaled Navier–Stokes equation is highly dependent on the value of the Reynolds number. If the Reynolds number is relatively small, which occurs in viscous fluids at low flow velocities, then the right-hand side of (4.119) dominates and the vorticity satisfies
∇
2
Ω ≈ 0
. For many boundary conditions this equation only has the solution
Ω = 0
, showing that viscous fluids flowing at low velocities often do so irrotationally, so that laminar flow persists. As R increases with high flow speeds and larger length scales, the left-hand side of (4.119) becomes important and the interaction of vorticity with the velocity field dominates the dynamics. This results in a much more complicated behavior of the vorticity and velocity field known as turbulence. Turbulence is characterized by large variations of the velocity field over small distances as well as the appearance of local angular momentum in the form of localized vortices, referred to as eddies, so that the flow appears chaotic. This explains why low-viscosity fluids, such as air and water, exhibit turbulent behavior under a wide variety of circumstances. Numerical analysis shows that for
R < 2000
laminar flow is stable, while for
R > 3500
turbulent flow sets in. Turbulence is characterized by a smooth fluid flow splitting into eddies. These eddies generate yet smaller eddies, giving rise to a process known as the energy cascade that eventually dissipates energy from the original laminar flow due to viscous forces at small scales. These eddies interact nonlinearly with one another, giving rise to a mathematically intractable situation. On the large scale, energy dissipates gradually, while on the small scale, the motion appears chaotic. Analyzing turbulent flow remains an open and important area of research beyond the scope of this text. The interested reader should consult the references.

sec.title: Homentropic flow
sec.p:
Because the action approach to dynamics is predicated on mechanical energy considerations, the presence of dissipative forces renders formulating an action approach difficult if not outright impossible. It was seen in several previous examples that the presence of viscosity removes mechanical energy from the fluid with no indication of how the mechanical energy is lost. This is identical to the effect that the dissipative force of kinetic friction has on the kinetic energy of a moving object. In typical physical systems the loss of mechanical energy is accompanied by the appearance of heat and temperature change. If
δ Q
heat flows into or out of the fluid or its subelements, then thermodynamic variables, such as temperature T, pressure P, and entropy S, are needed to specify how the conversion between heat and mechanical energy occurs. Stating these relations requires such properties as the thermal conductivity, heat capacity, and equation of state for the fluid, as well as the nature of the fluid’s environment. For that reason dissipative fluid flow can become extremely complicated. This section will limit consideration to a perfect fluid undergoing constant-entropy flow. It will be shown that a constant-entropy flow is consistent with ignoring the presence of viscosity, since the effects of heat production are suppressed. This allows an action approach to fluid flow, since the conserved mechanical energy can be used in formulating the action. Of course, it comes at the expense of ignoring important aspects of a real fluid, instead describing a fluid Feynman referred to as dry water.

sec.title: Fluctuations around solutions and stability
sec.p: The stability of solutions to the equations of motion is an important consideration in field theory. The Euler–Lagrange equations give a set of functions that yield an extremal value for the action, but whether they correspond to a stable configuration of the action is not clear. The question of stability can be answered by considering initially infinitesimal perturbations or fluctuations around the solutions and determining their behavior. If infinitesimal fluctuations grow arbitrarily large in magnitude either spatially or temporally, or are complex quantities for real fields, then the solution is, by definition, not stable against fluctuations. This is similar to considering the second derivative of a function at an extremum point to determine whether it corresponds to a maximum or minimum.

For the case that there is a collection of fields in the system, the fields are given an additional label,

In the case of fluid flow this was done in the definition (4.152) for the stress–energy tensor, where the index α stood for the five degrees of freedom in the homentropic Lagrangian (4.144). Classical field theory texts that cover the topic of fluid mechanics include
•
Soper D 2008 Classical Field Theory (New York: Dover)
•
Nastase H 2019 Classical Field Theory (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Physics-oriented monographs dedicated solely to fluid dynamics include
•
Batchelor G 1967 An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
•
Landau L and Lifschitz E 1987 Fluid Dynamics 2nd edn (Oxford: Pergamon)
•
Chorin A and Marsden J 1993 A Mathematical Introduction to Fluid Mechanics (Berlin: Springer)
•
Bennett A 2006 Lagrangian Fluid Dynamics (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Monographs that cover turbulence in fluid flow include
•
Feynman R, Leighton R and Sands M 1965 The Feynman Lectures on Physics vol II (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley)
•
Tennekes H and Lumley J 1972 A First Course in Turbulence (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press)
•
Davidson P 2015 Turbulence: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers 2nd edn (Oxford: Oxford University Press)

•

Choudhuri A 1998 The Physics of Fluids and Plasmas (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In this chapter a theory involving complex-valued fields will be developed, based on the requirement that the equation of motion is Galilean covariant. This means that the equation of motion for the complex-valued fields will take the same form for all observers related by a Galilean transformation, as opposed to a theory where the Lagrangian and equation of motion change form in different frames of reference.

body.p:
In the previous two chapters field theories have been developed by applying Newtonian physics to the motion of a medium, either the continuous string of chapter 3 or the fluid of chapter 4. Each medium was shown to support stable wave motion governed by an equation of motion of the form
□
v
˜
φ = 0
, where φ was a real scalar quantity describing the disturbance in the medium. In the cases of string waves and sound waves, the equations of motion were linear, and this allowed the principle of superposition to be applied. In addition, in both cases, the equation of motion changed form under a Galilean transformation. In particular, the one-dimensional string result (3.49) showed that the d’Alembertian
□
v
˜
factorized into two differential operators associated with differing speeds of propagation when considered in a frame of reference in motion relative to the medium of the string.

In this chapter a theory involving complex-valued fields will be developed, based on the requirement that the equation of motion is Galilean covariant. This means that the equation of motion for the complex-valued fields will take the same form for all observers related by a Galilean transformation, as opposed to a theory where the Lagrangian and equation of motion change form in different frames of reference. This is accomplished by using complex-valued fields, φ and
φ
*
, that are not scalars. Instead, their behavior under a Galilean transformation allows the equation of motion to take the same form in all Galilean inertial frames. The result is a field theory version of the Schrödinger equation without the strict probabilistic interpretation required by quantum mechanics. Instead, it models the behavior of a fluid of identical particles in the classical limit. By including an interaction term, the resulting field theory can be interpreted as a classical model of the much-studied quantum mechanical phenomenon of Bose–Einstein condensation. At extremely low temperatures a dilute gas of bosonic particles will condense into the lowest available energy, forming a macroscopic quantum state known as a Bose–Einstein condensate. The restriction to bosonic particles is necessary in order for them to share the same energy. While a detailed explanation of this phenomenon lies in the domain of multiparticle quantum mechanics, its classical field description is referred to as an effective field theory, since it encapsulates many of the associated quantum phenomena. It is useful in its own right and offers a reasonably easy description of sound waves and vortices in the condensate without the additional complexity that quantum mechanical analysis requires. However, in order to give an accurate description of Bose–Einstein condensation, it has to borrow some of the quantum mechanical properties of the constituent particles. This is detailed later. In addition, it results in a nonlinear field theory, a property of many field theories of relevance to particle physics.

If there are no interactions between the particles, then μ can be set to zero, since there is no additional energy associated with adding or subtracting particles from the volume element. However, if there are interactions among the particles, the term proportional to μ must be kept and its value determined from the energy of interaction. This is a key component of analyzing a Bose–Einstein condensate.

sec.title: Galilean covariance
sec.p:
One of the central themes in physics and field theories is how to compare measurements made by observers in relative motion. In the cases of the wave solutions for the stretched string and sound disturbances in a fluid, it was found that observers in relative motion with respect to the medium claimed that the speed of propagation differed according to Galilean relativity. However, in the case of the complex fields being considered here, result (5.2) for the particle density must be agreed upon by all observers. In addition, the momentum and energy associated with solution (5.10) must transform under a Galilean boost to reflect the Newtonian result. sec.title: Scattering and the Dirac delta potential
sec.p:
In order to model a Bose–Einstein condensate it is critical to include the effect of interactions among the particles. It will be assumed that the chief form of interaction is through short-range elastic collisions. An elastic collision is one in which the energy before and after the collision is the same. abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This chapter begins by considering the reasons for the need to alter the rules of relativity. The need for the revision had its origins in electromagnetic phenomena, in particular, the understanding of light as an electromagnetic wave. It is instructive to review the situation prior to the development of the special theory of relativity in order to understand the conceptual dilemma that physics faced.

body.p: Experimental observations in the latter part of the 19th century forced physicists to abandon Galilean relativity as a universal truth. Although this chapter concentrates on the structure of the special theory of relativity that replaced Galilean relativity, it begins by considering the reasons for the need to alter the rules of relativity. The need for the revision had its origins in electromagnetic phenomena, in particular, the understanding of light as an electromagnetic wave. Although chapter 9 is dedicated to electromagnetic phenomena, it is instructive to review the situation prior to the development of the special theory of relativity in order to understand the conceptual dilemma that physics faced.

sec.title: Maxwell’s equations
sec.p:
The formulation of the laws governing electric and magnetic phenomena consumed a roughly eighty-year span in physics, starting with the seminal work of Coulomb on electric force in 1785 and ending with Maxwell’s analysis of electromagnetic waves in 1865. By Maxwell’s time the concepts of electric charge q, the electric field
E ( r , t )
, and the magnetic field
B ( r , t )
were well established and experimentally quantified. Electric and magnetic fields were understood to be real-valued vector fields, created by the presence and the motion of electric charge. Electric charge was a quantifiable property of some inertial matter but, unlike mass, not all inertial matter exhibited this property. The presence and motion of electric charge, much like a fluid, is quantified in terms of an electric charge density scalar
ρ ( r , t )
and an electric current density vector
J ( r , t )
. The relations of the field vectors
E
and
B
to ρ and
J
and to each other are quantified by four fundamental laws, referred to as Maxwell’s equations due to his codification of them. In the absence of dielectric materials and using MKSA units, these four laws are given by 6.1

The first two equations have charge and current present and are referred to as the inhomogeneous equations. The second two have no reference to electric charge and are referred to as the homogeneous equations. The last equation, regarding the absence of pointlike magnetic field sources, can be viewed as an open question, although there has been no experimental evidence to date that magnetic monopoles exist. It is possible to alter Maxwell’s equations in the event that such particles are observed, and this is discussed in chapter 9.

It was later experimentally determined that there is a fundamental unit of charge, denoted by e, and all other observable charges are integer multiples of e. The numerous successful applications of Maxwell’s equations to physical systems left no one in doubt of their validity.

sec.title: The problem with electromagnetic waves
sec.p:
In the three previous chapters the waves that were analyzed represented the propagation of a disturbance in a medium. The string wave’s medium was simply the string, the sound wave’s medium was the fluid, and the number density fluctuation’s medium was the Bose–Einstein condensate. It was natural for 19th century physicists to consider that there might be a medium for the propagation of light. This medium would have to permeate all of space and transparent forms of matter, since light arrives from distant stars as well as passing through transparent materials. Such a medium did not appear to create any discernible impediment to the motion of matter. The medium for light was dubbed the luminiferous ether as a result of these ethereal qualities. However, it would then be the case that the speed of light is actually measured relative to the ether. It was shown earlier in (3.49) that the wave equation changes form under a Galilean transformation to an observer in motion relative to the medium of the wave disturbance. In the case of light an observer moving with velocity
v
o relative to the ether would measure the speed of a light wave moving in the same direction as the observer as c −
v
o . It was assumed that the Earth’s motion around the Sun through the sea of ether would create the situation of an observer moving relative to the medium. For such a case the ratio

One possible reconciliation was that the equations of (6.1) were not correct and that the correct versions would be invariant or covariant under a Galilean transformation. This idea gained no traction because of the overwhelming success that the equations of (6.1) had demonstrated in explaining numerous phenomena. There was a third possibility, which was that Galilean relativity was incorrect and needed to be replaced with a new version of relativity that would leave the equations of (6.1) the same for all observers. By the end of the 19th century it had been experimentally established that the observed speed of light c did not depend on motion relative to some medium and the ether concept was abandoned. There was no privileged observer and instead all inertial observers agree upon the form (6.1) for Maxwell’s equations. Therefore, the speed of light was the same for all observers, regardless of relative motion. It had become clear that Galilean relativity was incorrect. The dilemma facing physics was how to alter Galilean relativity and how to reconcile this alteration with Newtonian physics in a way that retained the successes of Newton’s laws of motion. The resolution came with Einstein’s publication of the special theory of relativity in 1905.

sec.title: Lorentz transformations
sec.p:
The first steps toward the special theory of relativity predated Einstein’s publication. In 1904, Lorentz derived a set of transformations which left Maxwell’s equations invariant in form and allowed the speed of light to be the same value c for all observers related by these transformations. It was unclear to physicists of the time what the meaning of the Lorentz transformations was. In 1905, Einstein showed that these same transformations could be derived by using simple algebraic manipulations of position x and time t, but only if the concepts of absolute time and length were abandoned. Instead, each individual inertial observer is equipped with a clock and meter stick to record the position x and time t of events. The identification of an inertial observer is made by determining that such an observer is moving at a constant velocity relative to all other inertial observers. It is the constant velocity requirement that makes this the special theory of relativity. It is natural to ask how many inertial observers there are. Both Newtonian physics and Mach’s principle treat the bulk matter of the Universe as defining an inertial frame, so that constant motion relative to the distant stars defines an inertial frame. Mach’s principle appears in general relativity, which includes arbitrary accelerated frames. Because Newton’s laws of motion were developed to reflect Galilean relativity, it becomes critical to understand how special relativity alters Newtonian mechanics into relativistic mechanics when accelerated objects are observed. Before proceeding to this goal, it is useful to understand some fundamental differences between special relativity and Galilean relativity.

sec.title: Observational effects of special relativity
sec.p: As mentioned earlier, embracing special relativity requires abandoning the concepts of absolute length and time. Using the Lorentz boosts of (6.30) to compare measurements of events yields results that are quite different from those of Galilean boosts. For simplicity, the effects on different observers’ measurements will be presented in the context of the one-spatial-dimension Lorentz boosts of (6.27).

which is the same effect. As a result, both observers will claim that the other’s clock is ticking slower. This gives rise to what is referred to as the twin paradox, asking which of two twin observers will really have less time go by according to the local clock as a result of relative motion. The resolution is to place both observers back into a common reference frame and compare their clocks. In order to do this, one or both of the observers must undergo a change in direction or magnitude of velocity, and this will break the symmetry between the two inertial observers and choose one or the other as having had less time elapse. The details of this are presented using the relativistic Doppler effect for light.
