Upon reunion, both agree that the rocket-based twin has aged 30 years, while the Earth-based twin has aged 50 years. It is important to note that the Earth-based twin will observe changes in the rocket-based twin’s signal frequency from a redshift to a blueshift, and this identifies the presence of an acceleration. The Earth-based twin is able to determine that no local acceleration effects occurred, which identifies the rocket-based twin as having undergone the acceleration. The rocket-based twin will observe the effects of the local acceleration that accompanied the return trip, in agreement with the Earth-based twin. As a result, the rocket-based twin is distinguished by not always being an inertial observer throughout the trip.

sec.p: The concept of space-time and the discovery that Lorentz boosts satisfy the multiplication rules of (6.51) and (6.53) opened the door to a profoundly deeper understanding of fundamental phenomena, such as electromagnetism and gravitation. When coupled with the geometric notation of chapter 1, it presents a much more compact and coordinate-free way of describing nature.

sec.title: Relativistic energy and momentum
sec.p:
Just as the Galilean boost played a key role in determining the form of Newton’s laws of motion, the Lorentz boost determines the structure of relativistic mechanics. All measurable quantities must have well-defined transformation properties, so that once they are known in one inertial frame, they can be found in all inertial frames by applying an appropriate Lorentz boost. In other words, all inertial observers agree on the measurable quantities and the equations of physics that govern them as well as how these quantities are related in different inertial frames. For velocities such that
v
/c is small, Newtonian quantities must reappear in order to preserve the successes of Newtonian mechanics.

The goal is to identify the relativistic generalizations of momentum and energy and eventually their relationship to force. This begins by deriving these generalizations for a free point mass using an action formulation. Motivation can be found in the earlier result (2.117), which showed that the Newtonian action for a free point mass was form invariant under a Galilean boost. By analogy, the relativistic action for a free point mass should be invariant under Lorentz transformations, since all inertial observers will agree that there is zero force acting on the particle. Having established the consistency of the relativistic version (6.137) of Newton’s second law, the next step is to identify the relativistic force

μ

This is not a trivial effort, since it requires finding a covariant expression for the particular force that reduces in the nonrelativistic limit to the Newtonian expression for the force as the gradient of a potential. It is further complicated by the fact that the Newtonian expression for the force may be incomplete or inconsistent with relativistic physics. A case in point is the gravitational force created by a moving mass. The change in the gravitational force it exerts on another body as a result of a change in its position is transmitted instantaneously throughout all of space if the Newtonian expression for the force is used. If the Newtonian expression were correct, then changes in the gravitational potential would travel faster than light. This is clearly inconsistent with the basic tenet of special relativity that the speed of light is the limit for the propagation of signals.

The position of the particle does not define an inertial frame, since, by definition, the particle is accelerated and therefore does not have a constant velocity relative to all inertial observers. Therefore, an inertial observer can measure the instantaneous velocity

( t )
of the particle and apply an instantaneous Lorentz boost to the particle’s rest frame force. This boost uses a time-dependent

in the Lorentz boost and will yield the force acting on the particle according to the inertial observer. The earlier results (6.118) and (6.119) show that this yields the correct time-dependent four-momentum appearing in (6.137). Such an instantaneous Lorentz boost with a time-dependent velocity no longer connects one inertial observer to another, since it does not obey condition (6.124). Instead, it connects the non-inertial frame of the particle to the frame of an inertial observer.

It is a natural question as to why applying an instantaneous Lorentz boost is the correct method to obtain the force on the particle. The answer is that the form of the Lorentz boost, even an instantaneous one, maintains the speed of light as a constant. As a result, the associated relativistic four-force in the inertial observer’s frame will be consistent with the basic postulate of special relativity. The limitation to one-dimensional or circular motion severely hampers the usefulness of static Newtonian potentials in a relativistic context. The fundamental forces of nature, such as gravity and electromagnetism, should yield expressions for motion that are covariant, so that all inertial observers agree upon them regardless of their relative velocity. It will be seen in chapter 9 that there is a Lorentz invariant velocity-dependent potential that reproduces the Lorentz force of electromagnetic phenomena for a relativistic point charge. This should not be a surprise, since Maxwell’s equations are a priori consistent with special relativity. However, the solution for gravity requires abandoning the Newtonian gravitational potential and introducing a space-time-dependent metric tensor. Chapter 10 examines the relativistic motion of a point particle in a gravitational field using the general relativistic extension of action (6.179). Fully describing the exchange of energy and momentum between matter and electromagnetic and gravitational fields requires the use of field theory to represent the matter, rather than relying on the mechanics of a point particle moving in a force field. In developing such a field theory the stress–energy tensor plays a key role in understanding the nature of the forces. This process began with the stretched string stress–energy tensor results (3.87) and (3.88), which were shown to be identical to the force and energy statements (3.71) and (3.76). The next step is to understand the stress–energy tensor as a relativistic statement. However, before doing so, a few simple examples of accelerated relativistic motion will be presented.

sec.title: Relativistic quantities
sec.p: In order to develop field theories that are consistent with special relativity, it is critical to identify the mathematical objects that have clearly defined Lorentz transformation properties. To do this properly requires the reader to be familiar with the basic aspects of group theory. This is presented in the next chapter after reviewing the requisite linear algebra and matrix manipulation. However, before developing those mathematical tools, it is still possible to identify some important relativistic quantities and relations—in particular, the relativistic form of the fluid stress–energy tensor.

Although neutrons decay into a proton, an electron, and a neutrino, the proton is stable within experimental limits. However, limiting consideration to the baryon density bypasses the mass conversion processes that take place in stellar interiors where light elements are fused into heavier elements. Although astronomical observations indicate the existence of dark nonbaryonic matter, baryonic matter accounts for the overwhelming bulk of the mass present in dense objects, such as planets and stars.

Most of the problems with the canonical stress–energy tensor of (6.242) arise because it is an ad hoc construction, having loosely evolved from the Euler–Lagrange equations of motion to represent a collection of conservation laws relating momentum and energy. It is important to develop the stress–energy tensor in a more systematic way. In the next chapter the stress–energy tensor and its associated conservation laws will be placed on a firmer basis through Noether’s theorem, where they are seen to originate from symmetries of the Lagrangian and the equations of motion obtained from it. Eventually a symmetric stress–energy tensor will be defined in chapter 10 by combining functional methods with general relativity.

The relativistic version of the symmetric fluid stress–energy tensor (4.170) is important in cosmology and astrophysical processes. The method for finding it is identical to the method used to find the relativistic force of (6.164) and (6.165). abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Identifying and classifying fundamental field theories is greatly facilitated by the mathematical tools of basic linear algebra and group theory. The reader familiar with these topics may wish to skip to the end of this chapter, where the properties of the Lorentz group are discussed and their representations are developed. Readers unfamiliar with these techniques can use the brief review of these methods presented in the first two sections to identify where further study is required.

body.p: Identifying and classifying fundamental field theories is greatly facilitated by the mathematical tools of basic linear algebra and group theory. The reader familiar with these topics may wish to skip to the end of this chapter, where the properties of the Lorentz group are discussed and their representations are developed. Readers unfamiliar with these techniques can use the brief review of these methods presented in the first two sections to identify where further study is required.

sec.title: Linear algebra and matrices

A matrix

In the case of a matrix these indices do not necessarily correspond to contravariant or covariant components, so that there is no need to distinguish superscript and subscript indices in that case. If the elements of a matrix are identified as being related to position or velocity vectors, then superscript and subscript indices are used. The definition of matrix multiplication creates the possibility that

The order of the three matrices in each term is a cyclic permutation of the previous term, where the last matrix in the previous term becomes the first matrix in the next term. The proof of (7.9) is straightforward, simply amounting to substituting the definition of each commutator into the appropriate expression and noticing that the twelve terms all cancel. The Jacobi identity is unique in the sense that there are no similar identities involving four or more matrices. This is because for n matrices there are

sec.title: Basic group theory
sec.p: Group theory has its origins in the classification of transformations and their relation to differential equations. This section provides a very brief and incomplete introduction to this rich subject, which is motivated by a study of finite matrix transformations. Consideration will be limited to what are called continuous Lie groups, since they form the basis of special relativity as well as nonabelian gauge field theories. Loosely speaking, a group is a collection of mathematical objects such that the product or composition of any two members of the collection yields another member of the collection. It also possesses an identity element so that its product with any member of the collection yields that member.

sec.title: Spatial rotations and continuous groups
sec.p: A simple and useful example of a group is the matrix representation of a transformation corresponding to the rotation of a coordinate system in a three-dimensional Euclidean space. The three Cartesian coordinates of a point can be viewed as the components of a contravariant position vector from the origin to the point. Since rotation is a type of coordinate transformation, it will be accompanied by a change in the components of the vector. The effect of rotating the x–y plane around the z-axis by the angle θ is depicted in figure 7.1.

caption.p: A right-handed rotation by the angle θ around the z-axis for the Cartesian coordinate system in a three-dimensional Euclidean space. The right triangles OAD, ABD, and PBC are all similar.

sec.p: Actively rotating the coordinate system through an angle θ counterclockwise around the z-axis causes the x and y coordinates of the point or equivalently the components of the position vector to change.

sec.p:
The commutation relations of (7.192) define the Lorentz algebra in four space-time dimensions. Any set of mathematical objects

It is instructive to note that the commutator of two boost generators yields a rotation, referred to as a Wigner or Thomas rotation. abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In this chapter Lorentz invariant field theories will be developed for the case that fields are scalar or spinor quantities. The action method used in previous chapters will be developed so that the action is invariant under the action of the Lorentz group. In so doing, the action of the Lorentz group will become a symmetry of the action, representing an action on the fields and their arguments that leaves the action invariant. As a result, all inertial observers will agree on the form of the action as well as the associated Euler–Lagrange equations of motion.

body.p: In this chapter Lorentz invariant field theories will be developed for the case that fields are scalar or spinor quantities. The action method used in previous chapters will be developed so that the action is invariant under the action of the Lorentz group. In so doing, the action of the Lorentz group will become a symmetry of the action, representing an action on the fields and their arguments that leaves the action invariant. As a result, all inertial observers will agree on the form of the action as well as the associated Euler–Lagrange equations of motion. Lorentz invariance is now understood to be a requirement for all fundamental field theories. ‘Fundamental field theory’ means a field theory representing a fundamental force present in the world. Although treating the world as built from point particles interacting with fields has proven to be an incomplete approach to fundamental interactions, it still yields important insights. As a result, this chapter will begin by defining the conserved currents and stress–energy tensor associated with charged and massive point particles. The next step is to understand what a Lorentz invariant action requires and then develop it for the case of scalar and spinor fields. The chapter concludes with the derivation of Noether’s theorem, which yields the conserved quantities associated with a symmetry or invariance of the action. In the case of scalar and spinor fields this allows the definition of conserved orbital angular momentum, and in the case of spinor fields it allows the definition of the intrinsic angular momentum, known as helicity.

sec.title: Lorentz invariant actions
sec.p: Field theories that describe the fundamental behavior of nature at arbitrary energies and velocities approaching c must be consistent with the rules of special relativity. The physical quantities modeled by a field theory must therefore have well-defined transformation properties for space-time coordinate changes. The second critical requirement of a fundamental field theory is that the equations of motion for the field theory take the same form for all inertial observers, as defined by special relativity. This means that a field theory’s equations of motion must also transform as a representation of the Lorentz group. This is often referred to as Lorentz covariance, but it is not directly related to covariant tensors. The first step in defining a relativistic field theory requires identifying the Lorentz invariant quantities to be used as the building blocks of the theory. This requires identifying the representation space to be used to define the Lorentz invariant quantities. The second step is to determine the equations of motion for these quantities that are both covariant and reflect experimentally observed qualities. The equations of motion are not Lorentz invariant, but they take the same form and hold in all inertial frames. The second step will hold if the equations of motion are derived from an action that is invariant under Lorentz transformations, so that the action is a Lorentz scalar. Lorentz invariance of the action determines a set of conservation laws via Noether’s theorem, which is to be discussed in a subsequent section.

The first step in this process is to note that the field theory actions developed in previous chapters were given by integrations over both space and time. In a four-dimensional world this means that the action will be given by 8.13

The alternative, allowing nonlocal interactions, often leads to a breakdown in causality in the relativistic case, a situation where events separated by space-like distances still influence one another. As a result, such theories will not be considered in the relativistic case. However, in the case where there are interacting fields, it is possible to create an effective field theory with nonlocal interactions, like the one considered in (5.93) describing the Bose–Einstein condensate. This will be discussed later when the effect of interactions is considered.

sec.title: Relativistic scalar field theory
sec.p:
A relativistic field theory can be formulated using a real or complex Lorentz scalar field

This means that another inertial observer, denoted by the prime, will use the same function φ but will transform the event x into their inertial frame using a Lorentz transformation,

There are results from quantum field theory that place limits on the possible powers of φ in order to correspond to a well-behaved theory. While any power of φ may appear in a classical theory, quantum field theories are limited to no higher than quartic powers. An action that is quadratic in the field variable will give an Euler–Lagrange equation that is linear in the field. Because such an equation satisfies the principle of superposition, its solutions can be used as a basis for more complicated field theories where terms higher than quadratic appear. For that reason, a quadratic action is the best starting point for constructing a field theory.

It was found experimentally that a scalar field was inadequate to describe the electron. This is discussed in a coming section where the Weyl and Dirac equations are developed. Since there was no experimentally known fundamental scalar field at the time, the Klein–Gordon equation appeared to have no immediate application. Subsequently, it was discovered that certain subatomic particles such as the pi meson are approximately scalar, in the sense that they are tightly bound pairs of quarks behaving like a scalar field, but complicated by the fact that they carry electric charge. Later, the Higgs field was proposed theoretically and then found to exist experimentally. As of this writing, the Higgs field is the only experimentally verified fundamental scalar field present in nature, although it is not the single real scalar field φ of (8.25). This is discussed in the final chapter of this book. Although the Higgs field can be treated as a classical field theory, ultimately it is quantum mechanical in nature and the

sec.title: Relativistic spinor fields and quadratic actions
sec.p:
In this section relativistically invariant actions for Weyl spinors and Dirac bispinors will be constructed using the results of the previous chapter, where spinor representations of the Lorentz group were developed. The key results necessary to introduce a Lorentz invariant action are (7.216) in the case of the Weyl spinor and (7.273) in the case of Dirac bispinors. These two results associate an inverse Lorentz transformation with the spinor transformation and allow the construction of Lorentz invariant actions using the gradient
∂

sec.title: Symmetry and conservation laws
sec.p:
So far many of the important concepts in classical field theory have been developed, but much of the presentation has lacked a unifying principle. In particular, the identification of conserved quantities, which are critical to the understanding of physical processes, has been ad hoc and primarily based on use of the Euler–Lagrange equations of motion to justify them. This is remedied by Noether’s theorem, which provides a systematic means of identifying conserved quantities in field theory. The key concept is that of symmetry. In the context of field theory, a symmetry means that the action defining the theory is invariant under a symmetry operation. For example, the action in a relativistic field theory is constructed to be a priori invariant under Lorentz transformations, so that Lorentz invariance is automatically a symmetry of the action. Typically, a symmetry of the action in a field theory can involve both a change in the form or components of the fields as well as in the arguments of the fields, as in the case of a spinor field Lorentz transformation,

The subscript α appearing on the field represents a set of indices labeling all possible independent degrees of freedom for the fields appearing in the action. The indices can include tensor indices, spinor indices, and isospin indices. Isospin indices label a collection of fields that share a set of common properties. The first use of isospin grouped the neutron and proton together into a doublet and referred to the doublet as the nucleon. This was useful for building a theory of the nucleus, since the neutron and proton share many similar properties, such as an almost identical mass as well as similar interactions with other particles. The concept of isospin symmetry underlies the current formulation of many subatomic processes using field theory.

statement.label: Exercise 8.15:
statement.p:
Show that the Weyl spinor

sec.p:
Because the spin contents of the two possible Weyl spinor fields are
±
1

ℏ
, the Weyl field is referred to as a spin-1/2 field. Chirality or handedness, as related to helicity, is an important aspect of the phenomena that can be modeled by a field theory. In the case of the Weyl equation the initial choice of chirality for the theory, either left- or right-handed, cannot be changed by a parity transformation, since there is no unitary transformation that represents a parity change. This follows from the impossibility of boosting into the frame of the Weyl spinor. A Weyl spinor field therefore has a definite chirality that coincides with its helicity. The neutrino has a helicity identical to the Weyl spinor ξ, since it is only left-handed. If it is massless, the neutrino field is an ideal candidate for being modeled by the Weyl spinor ξ. However, current experimental evidence indirectly indicates a tiny but non-vanishing mass for the neutrino. The reasons for this tiny mass are a subject of much current research.

The electron has values for helicity like that of a Weyl spinor. However, unlike the Weyl spinor, it is massive and it is therefore possible to boost into a frame where the momentum of the electron switches sign. The electron must therefore be modeled with both chiralities, and this requires the use of a Dirac bispinor. For rotation only, the Lorentz transformation for a bispinor (7.264) becomes 8.265

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The primary purpose of this chapter is to present the structure of electrodynamics as a relativistic field theory, the underlying symmetry of gauge invariance, and the nature of electrodynamic force and energy.

body.p: The development of classical electrodynamics in the 19th Century revolutionized physics. Not only did it provide a set of mathematical tools that have explained a vast array of physical phenomena, but also, as shown in chapter 6, Maxwell’s equations and their predictions also forced the development of special relativity, which underpins the conceptual basis of modern physics. The primary purpose of this chapter is to present the structure of electrodynamics as a relativistic field theory, the underlying symmetry of gauge invariance, and the nature of electrodynamic force and energy. Many of the important physical phenomena that classical electrodynamics explains will unfortunately be omitted, and the reader is referred to the bibliography.

sec.title: Natural units
sec.p:
There are a number of natural constants that occur regularly in relativistic field theories. Chief among these are
ℏ
and c. Although these constants are useful they can become clutter in the formulas that occur. For that reason it is common to set them to unity and measure all physical quantities in either energy or length. This is referred to as the use of natural units. For the case of electrodynamics the scaling of (9.1) shows how the
E
and
B
fields can be measured in inverse length squared. Similarly, the current
J
μ
is measured in inverse length cubed, while the gauge field
A
μ
is measured in inverse length.

For the four-dimensional relativistic fields discussed so far, the scalar and vector fields have units of inverse length, while the spinor fields have units of inverse length to the 3/2 power. However, these fields and their derivatives and integrals are often used to calculate energy, momentum, and angular momentum, and it is important to understand how the units of length are converted into the relevant physical units of a particular system, such as SI or the centimetre–gram–second (cgs) system. This requires the appropriate use of factors of
ℏ
and c to convert the results found into the relevant physical quantities.

The conservation of the Noether current associated with invariance under rotations was used in (8.245) to derive the nonrelativistic expression for the orbital angular momentum of the scalar field. In that case, the asymmetric form of the stress–energy tensor appeared. The symmetry of the stress–energy tensor derived in the previous section allows the definition of a relativistic expression for the angular momentum of a field. sec.title: Spinor field angular momentum
sec.p:
It is natural to consider analyzing the angular momentum of the Dirac spinor field by a similar method. Taking such an approach immediately encounters the problem generated by the asymmetric nature of the spinor stress–energy tensor. The asymmetry of the spinor stress–energy tensor (9.153) results in an expression for the tensor (9.193) that generalizes angular momentum that is not conserved. In this section a symmetric spinor stress–energy tensor will be defined by symmetrizing (9.153) for the case of the non-interacting spinor field using the method of (9.162). The quantity E

. This creates a mathematically undefined quantity and therefore a result with no physical interpretation. Historically, this dilemma arose from treating the electron as a point particle, so that the limit

was believed to reflect the correct experimental nature of the electron. In the latter part of the 19th century and well into the 20th century, numerous attempts were made, particularly by Lorentz, to remedy this problem on a classical level by replacing the point charge with finite-sized or extended charge distributions. These models encountered additional problems when such extended charges had to incorporate the self-force created by the charge distribution on itself. Special relativity brought a further complication in that the shape of a moving extended charge distribution was dependent on its relative velocity, altering the self-force and self-energy. In addition, a moving charge receives a contribution to its momentum from the effective inertia of its self-energy,

Eventually, the development of quantum electrodynamics in the mid-20th Century provided a means to deal with the problems of self-interaction and infinite self-energies using the systematic methods of renormalization. For the purposes of this text, the classical self-energy problem will be ignored and the interested reader is referred to the references.

sec.title: Magnetic monopoles
sec.p:
One of Maxwell’s equations states that 9.436
∇ · B = 0 ,
which is the magnetic counterpart of Gauss’s law, 9.437
∇ · E =
J
0
.
While pointlike sources of the electric field are readily available in the laboratory, there has never been a reproducible observation of a pointlike source of magnetic field, the so-called magnetic monopole, despite extensive searches. Magnetic materials, such as ferromagnets, are always dipolar in nature, presenting north and south poles that cannot be separated by breaking the magnet in half. Upon breaking a ferromagnet in half the result is two dipolar ferromagnets.

Nevertheless, (9.436) should be viewed as a law that is consistent with current observations. However, it plays a central role in defining the gauge field A
μ , since 9.438

The combination of the gauge field and the gauge invariance of its equations of motion has become a linchpin of modern physics and provides critical guidelines for the description of other naturally occurring forces. The question of why there are no magnetic monopoles remains an open area of conjecture. It is possible that magnetic monopoles are simply extremely rare, due to conditions present in the early stages of the Universe. This is one of the possible outgrowths of the inflationary Big Bang model of the early Universe. This model is discussed briefly in the next chapter.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Special relativity consists of the set of Lorentz transformations that connects inertial frames, those moving with constant relative speed, in a manner that leaves the speed of light invariant. The universal laws of nature are required to take the same form in all such inertial frames. This is nothing more than Galileo’s principle revised to respect the invariance of the speed of light. These laws must therefore be stated in terms of mathematical objects that transform as a representation of the Lorentz group, and these are the scalars, spinors, and vectors of earlier chapters.

body.p:
Special relativity consists of the set of Lorentz transformations that connects inertial frames, those moving with constant relative speed, in a manner that leaves the speed of light invariant. The universal laws of nature are required to take the same form in all such inertial frames. This is nothing more than Galileo’s principle revised to respect the invariance of the speed of light. These laws must therefore be stated in terms of mathematical objects that transform as a representation of the Lorentz group, and these are the scalars, spinors, and vectors of earlier chapters. The first term on the right-hand side of (10.5) is the usual second-rank mixed tensor Lorentz transformation rule, while the second term is new.

This is similar to the result obtained from Newtonian mechanics, where the non-Galilean transformation of (2.30) altered the nature of the force acting on an object. In that case a transformation to an appropriate accelerated frame was shown in (2.34) to cancel the effects of a local gravitational force for all comoving inertial masses, regardless of their mass, as long as the inertial mass and the gravitational mass are the same. This gave rise to the concept of a freely falling frame of reference, where the measurable effects of gravity are absent. Another way of saying this is that a freely falling object will follow a trajectory independent of its inertial mass. This has come to be known as the weak principle of equivalence, since it assumes that inertial mass and gravitational mass are the same.

Similarly, an accelerated frame of reference can give rise to effects identical to a local gravitational force. Einstein argued that a person in a closed elevator cannot tell if objects are falling in the elevator because of the elevator’s acceleration or because of a nearby gravitating mass. Ignoring some subtleties, the Einstein principle of equivalence states that an accelerated frame of reference in the absence of all forces and the motion of an object in a gravitational field cannot be distinguished from each other by performing local experiments. This principle led Einstein to argue that including gravitation in field theories requires the equations of motion to remain form invariant under general coordinate transformations, which are referred to as diffeomorphisms. Loosely speaking, a diffeomorphism is a change of coordinates that is differentiable, single valued, and invertible, but otherwise arbitrary. Only a theory allowing this larger group of transformations would have the ability to transform away the effects of a gravitational field, at least locally, by an appropriate choice of accelerated frame.

Finally, the strong principle of equivalence includes both the weak and Einstein principles of equivalence. It includes the postulate that the gravitational motion of a small test body depends only on its initial position in space-time and its velocity, and not on its constitution, as well as the postulate that the outcome of any local experiment in a freely falling frame of reference is independent of the velocity of the laboratory and its location in space-time. These additions become significant in astronomical bodies such as neutron stars, where there is a significant level of binding energy due to gravitational attraction. Using mass and energy equivalence, such gravitational binding energy could affect the nature of gravitational interaction.

A theory including gravitation must also have a well-defined set of quantities that reflect the effects of gravitation on matter and energy in a manner that is also consistent with the invariance of the finite speed of light. The non-relativistic limit of these effects must be consistent with Newtonian gravitation. Finally, such a theory must reduce to the case of special relativity in the absence of a gravitational field or in a freely falling frame. A gravitational field theory must quantify the relationship between gravitation and general frames of reference, and so this version of gravitation has come to be known as general relativity. General relativity is an extremely rich subject, and the brief discussion presented in what follows can only sketch its foundations and some of its more famous ramifications.

Riemann and Gauss showed that the metric tensor is the key to defining differential geometry for curved manifolds, where it generalizes the Pythagorean theorem of flat space. It will be seen that the gravitational motion of point masses can be determined solely from the metric tensor in a Riemannian manifold. Since all point masses experience the same metric tensor, they will move identically in a gravitational field, just as they do in Newtonian gravity. The results of this section show that it is consistent with the principle of equivalence to identify
g
μ ν
( x )
as the agent of gravitation. There is a set of inertial or freely falling frames at every point where
g
μ ν
( x )
becomes the Minkowski metric,
η
μ ν
, and its first derivative vanishes in the neighborhood of x. This does not mean that the metric becomes the Minkowski metric everywhere after the transformation. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the metric tensor will typically vary from point to point, and a different inertial frame must be chosen at each space-time point. This simply reflects the fact that the force of gravitation can vary from point to point. As a result, only freely falling observers at the same point will agree on the relative speed of two particles. This result is very different from special relativity, where inertial frames at two different space-time points are related by a Lorentz transformation that enables the two inertial observers to compensate for their relative motion. In the presence of gravitation the inertial frames at two different space-time points are no longer simply related if there is a difference in the metric between the two points.

The covariant derivative of a vector is therefore different from a scalar, since vectors are defined in the tangent space that exists at each point in a manifold. Obtaining the derivative of a vector requires finding the change in the vector between two infinitesimally separated points, and therefore the two vectors being compared are defined in different tangent spaces. In the case of curved or non-Euclidean manifolds, such as the circle and the sphere, the tangent spaces were depicted in figure 1.5, explicitly showing that tangent spaces at different points are no longer parallel. The vector in the tangent space at

A pair of extremely important points emerge from (10.75) and (10.76). The first is that the affine connection (10.76) vanishes if a Lorentz transformation is chosen, since the Lorentz transformation obeys (6.90), which requires its second derivative to vanish. The affine connection (10.76) has therefore emerged from a transformation to a non-inertial frame. The second is that the Einstein principle of equivalence then states that a non-vanishing affine connection will be present in the case of a gravitational field. It should be mentioned that nonzero torsion is postulated to be present in some variants of Einstein’s version of general relativity, beginning with what is known as Einstein–Cartan general relativity. In these variants there are properties of matter, such as the spin of fermions or the rotation of a massive body, that act as the source of torsion even in freely falling frames. Since Einstein’s version of gravitation assumes that torsion vanishes, the presence of torsion in these theories results in a deviation from the predictions of Einstein’s gravitation for numerous physical phenomena, such as the precession rate of gyroscopes. However, the current measured deviations from Einstein’s gravity all lie within the error limits of the experimental apparatus, so that there is no experimental indication at this time that Einstein’s version of gravitation is incorrect. For completeness, torsion will be retained in further developments.

If the metric tensor is constant everywhere then the Levi-Civita connection vanishes, rendering the Riemann curvature tensor computed from it zero everywhere. Solely using the Levi-Civita connection yields a flat Riemannian manifold if the metric tensor is constant. sec.title: The connection and curvature in differential geometry
sec.p: The definition and use of the affine connection and the curvature in coordinate notation is accompanied by a proliferation of indices which can be cumbersome and mistake prone. Modern differential geometry allows a much more streamlined version of these definitions and relationships by adapting them to forms and coordinate-free notation. Since these techniques are often overlooked or introduced without explanation in physics texts, this section will present a reasonably concise introduction, drawing on the concepts of tensors and forms defined in chapter 1.

sec.title: Variational techniques in general relativity
sec.p:
Apart from the principle of equivalence very little of this chapter has considered the physics embodied in general relativity. In that regard the goal of modern field theory is to derive its equations of motion from the variation of an action that reflects the symmetries of the physical system under consideration. The principle of equivalence has led inexorably to the conclusion that a theory of gravitation requires its associated action to be invariant under general coordinate diffeomorphisms and that
g
μ ν
is the field of gravitation. In order to define the action it is necessary to have a relevant definition of
ℏ
, similar to the definition (9.88) made for electrodynamics. Using Newton’s universal gravitational constant G, it follows that
ℏ
can be defined in terms of an inertial mass M as 10.282
ℏ =
GM
2
c

However, unlike the case of electrodynamics and the fundamental charge e, there is no obvious fundamental mass M that occurs in nature. In other words, the particle masses occurring in nature are not integer multiples of some fundamental mass, in contrast to the electric charges that occur, which are integer multiples of a fundamental charge. Instead, G, c, and Planck’s constant
ℏ
are combined to form what is called the Planck length, 10.283

in SI units. This length is generally believed to be the scale of quantum gravity, a topic of considerable research and far outside the scope of this book. As a result, Planck’s constant will be used to create a dimensionless action.

sec.title: Einstein’s field equation
sec.p:
All the necessary tools for working with gravitation have been assembled, except for the equations that determine the metric tensor. To qualify, general relativity’s equations must yield Newtonian gravitation in the non-relativistic limit. In Newtonian physics it is the presence of inertial mass that is responsible for gravitation. Since special relativity shows the equivalence of mass and energy, it is logical to expect that in a relativistic version of gravity, both mass and energy act as the source of gravitation. This indicates a central role for the stress–energy tensor, which has already emerged in (10.347) by varying
g
μ ν
in the action for the matter fields. Therefore, unlike Einstein’s original derivation of the field equations, a variational approach will be used to derive the equations of motion.

sec.title: The variational approach
sec.p:
The action for gravitation must be a scalar under diffeomorphisms. The goal is to generate an equation of motion that is a second-order partial differential equation that couples
g
μ ν
to matter and energy and reduces to Newtonian gravitation in the non-relativistic limit. Such a theory must involve the Riemann curvature tensor, since it alone determines the true presence of curvature and therefore gravitation. The simplest possible choice for the Lagrangian

G
of gravity that meets these requirements is proportional to the Riemann curvature scalar, 10.364

G
= − κ R ,
where κ is a constant that is determined by matching the results to Newtonian gravity in the weak gravitational limit. This choice for the Lagrangian is referred to as the Hilbert action for gravitation and is not unique. Numerous modifications of the Hilbert action have been made over the years in an effort to determine whether they better fit observational data. The choice of the Hilbert action sets the units of κ by the requirement that
κ R
have the units of inverse length to the fourth power. Since
g
μ ν
is a dimensionless quantity, the definitions of the Riemann curvature tensor (10.209) and the Riemann curvature scalar (10.229) show that R has the units of inverse length squared due to the presence of second derivatives. Therefore, κ must have the units of inverse length squared or an inverse area.

caption.p: An interferometer for observing gravitational waves.

sec.p:
It is widely believed that the gravitational waves of general relativity can be viewed as composed of gravitons, which would be the counterpart to the photon of electromagnetic waves. Like electromagnetic waves, the gravitational wave travels at the speed of light and therefore the constituent gravitons would need to be massless. At the time of writing, unlike the case of electromagnetism, a consistent quantized version of general relativity does not exist, despite strenuous efforts to develop it. The primary problem in quantizing gravitation is the extreme nonlinearity of the Einstein equation of motion. In the case of electromagnetism the interaction term is linear in the gauge field which, by comparison, is much simpler than the nonlinear terms involving the metric tensor in the Ricci tensor. The problem is compounded by the weakness of the gravitational force compared to hadronic and electromagnetic interactions, which makes the experimental detection of a single graviton virtually impossible. For example, in SI units the gravitational force between two protons separated by the distance r is given by 10.443

The electric force completely dominates the interaction of charged inertial masses. In the case of protons there is also a hadronic force even stronger than the electric force for close separations.

In chapters 8 and 9 it was shown that fields may possess an intrinsic angular momentum, referred to as spin or helicity. In natural units the spinor field representing electrons has a helicity of
±
1

, while the helicity of the gauge field representing photons is ±1. The identification of these quantities as the spin projection of particles comes from the successful quantization of the associated field theories and the experimental measurement of the intrinsic angular momentum of these particles. However, the helicity results of the spinor and vector fields can be anticipated using classical field theory by applying Noether’s theorem to the normalized classical waves associated with these fields. In the case of electromagnetism the spin or helicity of the photon was identified classically by analyzing circularly polarized waves written in terms of the gauge field. Since the weak field metric tensor is the quantity that is propagating in a gravitational wave, it is straightforward to analyze the rotational content of the graviton, since the rotated metric tensor transforms according to 10.446

sec.title: Kaluza–Klein theory
sec.p: One of the earliest attempts at unifying forces originated with the work of Kaluza and Klein, who focused on unifying gravitation and electromagnetism in a geometric framework similar to general relativity. They used a five-dimensional variant of Einstein’s theory of gravitation to include electromagnetism as a geometric effect.

The basic idea is to expand the number of space-time dimensions from four to five by adding a fourth spatial dimension that is compact on a very small scale. The Kaluza–Klein mechanism is easily understood in the case of a cylindrical manifold where there are two spatial dimensions, the x-coordinate, with an infinite range, and the y-coordinate, a circular dimension characterized by the radius R. The y-coordinate can be replaced by the angular coordinate θ, so that

The Kaluza–Klein approach has also been adapted to Yang–Mills field theories, which are discussed in the next chapter, by increasing the number of compact dimensions. It is also used in string theory, where the extra dimensions needed to make string theory consistent quantum mechanically can be hidden through the compactification process.

sec.title: Basic cosmology
sec.p: Despite being the weakest of the natural forces, gravitation is the dominant force at the largest scales of the Universe. Not only is it long ranged, but unlike the only other long ranged force, electromagnetism, it is solely attractive and therefore cannot be screened. Soon after its inception Einstein’s version of gravity was applied to the large-scale behavior of the Universe, ushering in the era of scientific cosmology.

sec.title: The cosmological principle
sec.p: The application of general relativity to cosmology depends critically on observational astronomy, which has determined that, at very large scales, the visible part of the Universe is virtually isotropic and homogeneous in its mass distribution. This has been elevated to the cosmological principle, which states that all observers, regardless of location, will agree on the large-scale isotropic and homogeneous nature of the Universe, and that there is no preferred observer in the grand scheme of things. This restricts the spatial metric of the Universe to one of three possibilities, uniform and infinite in volume, uniform and finite in volume, or uniform and neither infinite nor finite in volume. These three options are referred to as open, closed, and flat. Each of these three possibilities can be modeled using a reasonably simple metric.

Before finding the form of the three possible metrics, it is important to characterize the stress–energy tensor for the uniformly distributed mass and energy of the Universe. Typically, this is done by using the stress–energy tensor for a non-interacting electrically neutral isotropic and homogeneous fluid, referred to earlier as a perfect fluid. This shows that a is an increasing function of time and that the second term on the right-hand side will therefore tend to zero, so that an open Universe dominated by vacuum energy will also enter a de Sitter phase and quickly become identical to a flat Universe dominated by vacuum energy. The deviation from the flat-space Universe is then quickly driven to zero. A period of inflation early in the history of the Universe, lasting roughly

It would also explain the absence of magnetic monopoles, which would have become separated before standard matter coalesced. The details of this are in the references. Extremely large vacuum energy density terms naturally occur in the physics of elementary particles, and so quantum field theory has direct implications for early cosmology. It is argued that in the early Universe the temperature was high enough to force the inflaton field into a metastable state, and the energy density of the field is estimated to have been on the order of

However, it is important to note that some physicists have been critical of the inflationary model. One of the more pressing difficulties in modeling inflation is to find a mechanism that allows inflation both to occur early in the evolution of the Universe and then to terminate, leading to the current state of the Universe, where inflation is not present. Such a mechanism is tied to the quantum behavior of fields under extreme conditions, and there are many computational and conceptual difficulties. It also often requires fine tuning of the initial conditions and the dynamics, a situation that has led some to reject inflation as an extremely improbable occurrence in the early Universe. Others remain confident in the viability of inflation. The interested reader is referred to the literature.

It is possible to model a static Universe by introducing a negative vacuum energy density that is exactly opposite to the matter and radiation energy density of the Universe at some point in its evolution. When the scale factor a reaches a value where the right-hand side of the Friedmann equation vanishes, then

Even if inflation did not occur, this eventually leads back to a moment where the volume of the Universe is so small and its contents so hot that the known behaviors of matter and energy break down. This is the moment that early critics of the idea derisively referred to as the Big Bang, a name which has stuck. In order to trace back any further requires an understanding of quantum gravity, and such a theory is currently not available in a consistent form.

In effect, the blackbody radiation that was present would decouple from matter, since only those wavelengths corresponding to atomic spectra would be absorbed and scattered. The details of this depend on the quantum mechanical absorption and emission spectrums of the atomic matter that had formed.

As it continued to expand, the Universe became dominated by matter, while the decoupled blackbody radiation underwent an increase in wavelength as the scale of the Universe increased. This ambient blackbody radiation has been detected and is remarkably uniform, coming from all directions in the sky in concordance with the cosmological principle. It now lies in the microwave spectrum, corresponding to blackbody radiation at
T = 2.7
K
, revealing that the Universe has increased in scale by over a factor of 103 since atomic matter first formed. Initially predicted by Alpher and Herman in 1948 and later observed in 1965 by Penzias and Wilson, it is known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and carries information about the earliest stages of the Universe after the Big Bang. Its extreme uniformity provides experimental support for the occurrence of an inflationary period in the early Universe. The subsequent evolution of the Universe was the result of a combination of vacuum energy and matter. Using a combined energy model, the current age of the Universe is estimated at 10.584

In the time since the Big Bang, the greatest distance light could have traveled is therefore 14 billion light-years or about 4000 megaparsecs. This constitutes the observable size of the Universe, and is referred to as the cosmic horizon.

Many theoretical questions and experimental uncertainties remain; in particular, the observationally inferred existence of dark matter and dark vacuum energy. Dark matter does not interact with light as the visible matter of galaxies and interstellar space does, but its presence and its inertial mass have been inferred from the anomalous rotation rates for galaxies. Similarly, dark vacuum energy has been inferred from the redshifts of type I supernovas, which indicate the expansion rate of the Universe is increasing. These two sources of gravitation will play a key role in determining the past as well as the future of the Universe. As the time of writing, these forms of energy and matter have yet to be experimentally identified and are an open theoretical question.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: A major theme in physics has been the identification of similarities or symmetries in the patterns of naturally occurring forces. In the subatomic realm this classificationscheme goes by the general name of isospin. In its earliest form the similarities between the neutron and proton allowed them to be treated as two manifestations of the nucleon. The neutron bispinor n and proton bispinor p were grouped together into an isospin doublet (n p), in effect a matrix vector built from the two bispinors. This led to the generalization of electric charge, as well as the exploration of how the nucleon doublet entered into interactions with itself and other particles. In the process, physicists understood how the gauge symmetry and gauge field of electrodynamics could be generalized to isospin, and this gave rise to the extremely important concept of the Yang–Mills field.

body.p:
A major theme in physics has been the identification of similarities or symmetries in the patterns of naturally occurring forces. In the subatomic realm this classification scheme goes by the general name of isospin. In its earliest form the similarities between the neutron and proton allowed them to be treated as two manifestations of the nucleon. The neutron bispinor n and proton bispinor p were grouped together into an isospin doublet
( n
p )
, in effect a matrix vector built from the two bispinors. This led to the generalization of electric charge, as well as the exploration of how the nucleon doublet entered into interactions with itself and other particles. In the process, physicists understood how the gauge symmetry and gauge field of electrodynamics could be generalized to isospin, and this gave rise to the extremely important concept of the Yang–Mills field. Subsequently, it was found that electrodynamics, general relativity, and Yang–Mills fields share many similar structures, in particular, the presence of a connection, and can be expressed in terms of forms and curvature. In what follows, natural units are employed, where all powers of
ℏ
and c are suppressed, and it is assumed that all fields, masses, and energies are expressed in terms of powers of inverse length.

Λ
a
and is therefore not unique. In that regard, Yang–Mills theory was not developed from a body of experimental observations of reproducible phenomena as electrodynamics was. Instead, it is a theoretical extension of abelian gauge theory and its connection to experiment has arisen from observations of particle processes modeled by using a Yang–Mills theory to define a quantum field theory. This is the principal reason that most attention has been focused on the quantum properties of Yang–Mills field theories rather than on their classical behavior.

A very successful use of Yang–Mills fields is that of the electroweak (Glashow–Weinberg–Salam) theory, in which both the electromagnetic and the weak force are united as manifestations of an
SU
( 2 )
× U
( 1 )
gauge theory. The three gauge fields associated with
SU
( 2 )
and the one gauge field associated with
U
( 1 )
combine into the massless photon and three massive vector particles through an effect known as the Higgs mechanism. This is presented in a later section. Another application is the quark model of hadrons, which postulates that hadronic matter is composed of spinor particles, known as quarks, interacting through Yang–Mills gauge fields, known as gluons. The theory is known as quantum chromodynamics and derives its name from the assumption that there are three colors of quarks—the name for the index of the isospin triplet of spinor fields—that form the representation space for the gauge group
SU
( 3 )
. Single quarks are never observed, and there are strong indications that the nonlinear nature of the gluonic fields creates an effect known as confinement, with the result that all hadronic matter consists of pairs and triplets of quarks. In particular, the quantum mechanical result known as asymptotic freedom shows that the effective coupling constant g in the quantum field theory becomes negligible at high momentum or, equivalently, short distances. Much effort has gone into extracting the hadronic spectrum from the associated Yang–Mills quantum field theory, primarily through numerical simulation of quantum processes via lattice gauge theory. Of the two theories, the electroweak model is arguably better understood, since its particle processes are both theoretically well-defined and accessible through experiment. Some aspects of the
SU
( 2 )
version of classical quantum chromodynamics are discussed in a later section.

However, there are several important problems with this procedure that must be dealt with. The spin of the massless abelian gauge field discussed in chapter 9 was the result of circular polarization for the electromagnetic wave, and it was shown in (9.310) that there are only two helicities available, corresponding to

Since a massive gauge field no longer travels at the speed of light, it is possible to boost into the frame of a circularly polarized wave, so that there is no longitudinal momentum, resulting in a spin projection or helicity that is zero. sec.title: Yang–Mills fields and the Gribov instability
sec.p:
The theory known as quantum chromodynamics is an
SU
( 3 )
gauge theory. In its fundamental representation it describes three spinor quarks interacting through the eight gauge fields referred to as gluons that are associated with the eight generators of
SU
( 3 )
. It is generally believed that this theory underlies hadronic physics, explaining the extensive variety of strongly interacting massive particles, ranging from nucleons to the scalar and vector mesons detected in interactions. However, single quarks have never been detected in any experiments, and there are indications from the quantum version of the theory that the gluons create an interaction that grows with separation, so that the quarks are confined into pairs and triplets. Lattice gauge analysis of the quantum theory indicates that nonabelian magnetic effects may be responsible for creating such a confining potential, but the details of this remain unclear at this time.

Analysis of this problem in the research literature has focused on the role of quantum mechanical effects in this process. Since this is a monograph on classical field theory, it is meaningful to ask if there is any insight into this problem at the classical level. In regard to that question, this monograph will focus on the classical version of what is called the Gribov instability. In the context of the quantum theory, Gribov demonstrated that the Coulomb phase of quantum chromodynamics is unstable for strong coupling. This can be interpreted as a need to replace the Coulomb potential by a confining potential, often modeled as a flux tube joining the quarks into a bound state. The analysis to be presented here supports the existence of the Gribov instability, even at the classical level. For simplicity, this will be demonstrated for the case that the gauge group is reduced to
SU
( 2 )
with three gauge fields interacting with a spinor doublet.

In earlier analysis of abelian gauge theory the Coulomb potential emerged by solving the classical equation of motion in the presence of a static point charge, while the Coulomb force was understood by considering the field (9.359) around a static charge pair. A similar approach will now be taken in the nonabelian case. Before proceeding it is important to note that the stress–energy tensor analyzed earlier shows that the force density equations generated by static charges are formally similar in both the abelian and nonabelian cases. The solution to (11.212) for the case of point charges gave rise to the Coulomb potential in (9.359). Therefore, it would appear that the Coulomb potential and force are also the solution for the Yang–Mills case. Since the Coulomb potential definitely does not confine electric charge, it is natural to conclude that reducing the Yang–Mills equations of motion to (11.212) must be an error, and that solutions involving the magnetic fields must be sought.

Unfortunately, there are no known analytical solutions to the equations of motion (11.52) that involve both the magnetic and electric fields in the presence of point charges. However, there is a reasonably simple way to investigate the effects of the nonabelian magnetic fields in shaping the nature of the force, and that is to consider magnetic fluctuations around the solution to (11.212). If these fluctuations are unstable, growing arbitrarily large or becoming complex, then the Coulombic solution (11.212) is not physically viable. This was done with fluids in chapter 4, where freely propagating density fluctuations or sound waves in a static fluid were found. In that case it meant that a static fluid was stable, since the sound waves, which carry energy, did not grow arbitrarily large spatially or temporally.

sec.title: Classical string theory
sec.p: String theory has its origin in the hadronic physics discussed in the previous section, where pairs of quarks are modeled as being confined through a string-like flux tube. As the confined pair moves, the string joining them traces out a surface. It was initially thought that the myriad of light mesons that occur in hadronic processes could be understood as excitation states of the quark pair plus the confining string. Such a string would have endpoints corresponding to the positions of the two point particle quarks, corresponding to an open string.

Whereas a point particle traces out a worldline as it moves, such an open string would trace out a surface or worldsheet as it moved, as depicted in figure 11.1. The action for a point particle can be viewed as the length of its worldline. This is most easily seen from the relativistic free point particle action (6.100), where 11.273

Treating the string as an object in and of itself shows that it need not be open. A much-studied object is the closed string, whose worldsheet is depicted in figure 11.1. sec.title: D-branes
sec.p:
Higher-dimensional objects are available in this approach to dynamics. For example, a two-dimensional surface that propagates is referred to as a membrane, and as it propagates it traces out a three-dimensional worldvolume, as depicted in figure 11.1. The Nambu–Goto action can be generalized to such p-dimensional objects by using the parameterization invariant worldvolume defined using the induced metric. For example, the membrane can be parameterized as 11.314

. A simple version of a membrane is described by a plane that is orthogonal to all but two of the spatial directions. For example, in a four-dimensional target space-time, the coordinate system can be chosen so that the membrane is perpendicular to the z-axis, in effect parallel to the x–y plane.

Like the open string the open membrane is finite in extension in both spatial directions. This requires a set of boundary conditions for the equation of motion generated by the action. Choosing Dirichlet boundary conditions led to the membrane being referred to as a D2-brane. Similarly, higher-dimensional objects are referred to as Dp-branes. One of the more intriguing aspects of Dp-branes is their interaction with open strings. Polchinski showed that open strings could bind to Dp-branes by choosing free endpoint boundary conditions for the brane coordinates and Dirichlet conditions for the coordinates orthogonal to the brane. In effect, the string endpoints are free to move in the volume of the brane. A simple example of this is given by an open string bound to a D1-brane, as depicted in figure 11.2. The D1-brane consists of a line in the y direction at a specific value of x. The string endpoint is free to slide in the y direction, but it cannot move in the x direction due to the Dirichlet condition (11.296). This has led to the interesting possibility that the particles that are present in the observed four-dimensional space-time are open strings bound to a D3-brane in a higher-dimensional Universe.

sec.p:
The application of unitary symmetry to particle physics originated with
•
Heisenberg W 1932 Z. Phys. 77 1
The development of local nonabelian gauge fields originated with
•
Yang C N and Mills R 1954 Phys. Rev. 96 379
Classical field theory texts that cover unitary symmetry include
•
Kosyakov B 2007 Introduction to the Classical Theory of Particles and Fields (Berlin: Springer)
•
Scheck F 2012 Classical Field Theory (Berlin: Springer)
•
Nastase H 2019 Classical Field Theory (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Most of the physical applications of unitary symmetry have been in the context of particle physics and its associated quantum field theory. As a result, the content of chapter 11 includes many concepts that are also available in quantum field theory textbooks, where they are often initially stated using a classical framework. This includes the development of nonabelian symmetry, Yang–Mills fields, spontaneously broken symmetry, and pure gauge solutions to the equations of motion. The reader interested in this perspective is referred to the following quantum field theory textbooks for useful insights into unitary symmetry in field theory and its pertinence to particle physics.
•
Peskin M and Schroeder D 1995 An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley)
•
Weinberg S 1996 The Quantum Theory of Fields vol II (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
•
Srednicki M 2007 Quantum Field Theory (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
•
Tully C 2011 Elementary Particle Physics in a Nutshell (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press)
Classical solutions to nonlinear field theory equations of motion are presented in detail in
•
Actor A 1979 Rev. Mod. Phys. 51 461
•
Rajaraman R 1987 Solitons and Instantons (Amsterdam: North-Holland)
Nonabelian gauge theory is presented in terms of differential forms in
•
Naber G 1997 Topology, Geometry, and Gauge Fields (Berlin: Springer)
•
Frankel T 1997 The Geometry of Physics (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
•
Nakahara M 2003 Geometry, Topology, and Physics 2nd edn (New York: Taylor and Francis)
The Gribov instability was first noted in
•
Gribov V 1977 Lecture at 12th Winter School of the Leningrad Nuclear Physics Institute (https://http://www.slac.stanford.edu/pubs/slactrans/trans01/slac-trans-0176.pdf)
•
Magg M 1978 Phys. Lett. B74 246
Classical string theory is presented in
•
Zweibach B 2004 A First Course in String Theory (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
•
Szabo R 2004 An Introduction to String Theory and D-brane Dynamics (London: Imperial College Press)
•
Schomerus V 2017 A Primer on String Theory (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
